research.summary:
The Tesla browser is a Chromium build that Tesla updates through its firmware. It went to Chromium 140 in 2026.14.3/.6 (April 2026) and 148 in 2026.26 (summer 2026). Engine features from Chrome 66 onward (AudioWorklet), Chrome 92 onward (SharedArrayBuffer with COOP/COEP) and WebGPU are therefore present in the engine. Only WebGPU is backed by Tesla's own wording. Nobody has published an in-car test of AudioWorklet, SharedArrayBuffer, Service Worker or the Fullscreen API.

Audio and driving:
- Browser audio keeps playing while driving. While the car moves, only the picture of a `<video>` element is suppressed; canvas and WebGL are not.
- Browser audio is its own media source. Per the owner's manual it keeps playing when the browser is minimised, shows in the Miniplayer, and the user's other media resumes when browser audio stops. So Tesbox will replace the user's music, not mix under it.
- The car changes media volume with driving speed.
- A tap is needed before audio can start, because of Chromium's autoplay policy.

Speed data: GPS arrives to the browser at about 1 Hz. On AMD Ryzen cars the position is the car's dead-reckoned fix and `coords.speed` is filled. On pre-2022 Intel Atom cars the speed reads zero or null and updates stop when the fix drops. Speed has to be worked out from position deltas there.

Breaking changes in 2026.26:
- The "Tesla/<firmware>" marker was removed from the user agent. The UA never identified the model or hardware anyway.
- The 3/Y page zoom went from devicePixelRatio 1.0 to about 1.53.
- The browser window shrinks while driving, to about 773×601 CSS px on 3/Y and 804×638 on the new Model Y.

Detection: hardware has to be detected from the WebGL renderer string and from screen size × devicePixelRatio, with the model chosen by the user.

Developers report these gotchas: watchPosition and DeviceOrientation crashing the tab, reloads mid-drive, memory pressure on Intel, no speechSynthesis voices, and an optional ad blocker that strips third-party scripts.

Connectivity: the browser needs Wi-Fi or a hotspot, or Premium Connectivity on cellular.

Tesla has no developer terms for in-browser web apps. The browser can be blocked through parental controls (2026.20 onward), and the manual warns against using the touchscreen while moving.

claims.claim: Tesla's in-car browser is Chromium-based. Update 2026.14.3 (released 2026-04-28; also listed as 2026.14.6) moved it from Chromium 136 to 140 on S, 3, X, Y and Cybertruck, with release-note wording that it 'improves WebGPU performance'.
The 2026.26 Summer Update (July–Aug 2026) moved the browser to a Chromium 148 engine. This comes from third-party measurement; Tesla's release notes give no number.

Chromium version history in the car: 75 (2019.40), 79 (2020.x), 88 (2021.x), 100 (2022.20), a jump in 2022.12.1, 136 by early 2026, 140 (2026.14), 148 (2026.26). Tesla ships months behind upstream Chrome.

Historical UA strings carried a firmware token, e.g. 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; GNU/Linux) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chromium/88.0.4324.150 Chrome/88.0.4324.150 Safari/537.36 Tesla/2021.36.5.5-c6d521764ab9' and 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) ... Chrome/100.0.4896.127 Safari/537.36 Tesla/feature-2022.20.9-31-abc'. None identified the model or MCU, and Intel and AMD both report x86_64.

The 2026.26 firmware removed the 'Tesla' marker from the browser UA and changed the reported screen size. Developers now detect the car from physical screen size and the in-car graphics chip (WebGL renderer). tesla-cloud saw the same thing: the UA changes across releases and the browser can look like a mobile device.

2026.26 turned on a browser-wide default page zoom. On Model 3/Y, devicePixelRatio went from 1.0 to about 1.53 and the CSS viewport from about 1920×1160 to about 1254×784 (parked). There is no user zoom control (no menu, shortcut or pinch).

The browser is not full-screen while driving and the viewport shrinks in motion. Measured on 2026.26 / Chromium 148: Model 3/Y 2020–25 about 773×601 CSS at dpr 1.53 in motion (1254×784 parked); new Model Y (Juniper, 16-inch 2560×1440 screen) 804×638 at dpr 1.96 in motion (about 1306×735 parked). The S/X 2021+ figure conflicts: about 1410×833 at dpr 1.56 in one source, 'unscaled' (dpr ~1) per codriver.
In the Tesla browser, pointer:fine and hover:hover are reported, maxTouchPoints is 16, and prefers-color-scheme reports light.

Hardware can be told apart by GPU and performance rather than by UA. Intel Atom (MCU2) is in pre-Dec-2021 Model 3/Y and 2018–2021 S/X; AMD Ryzen (MCU3) is in Model 3/Y from about Dec 2021, refresh S/X, and Cybertruck. AMD-only browser features exist: camera and mic in 2026.26.

WebGL/canvas performance (Aug 2026): a 2023 Model Y (AMD) holds a steady 60 fps for a custom WebGL 3D map. A 2019 Model 3 or 2017 Model S (Intel MCU2) manages 10–15 fps with a general-purpose map engine and 25–35 fps with a purpose-built renderer. Intel cars need very lean rendering.
Browser audio keeps playing while the car is in Drive or moving. Only the picture of a <video> element is suppressed (audio continues). <canvas> and WebGL drawing are not suppressed in motion.

Owner's manual: when you play audio through the web browser and minimise the browser, the car keeps playing it in the background. It can be paused or played from the media Miniplayer. If other media was playing before browser audio began, that media resumes after browser audio pauses or ends. Browser audio therefore takes over the media source; it does not mix with or duck the user's music.

Owner's manual: media volume 'may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings', and audio volume may drop briefly when shifting into Reverse. The car's own speed-dependent gain sits on top of whatever Tesbox outputs.

Left scroll button on 3/Y-class cars: press = play/pause media, tilt left/right = previous/next track, roll = system volume, long press = custom shortcut, both pressed = gear selector/restart. For a page playing an <audio> element, Tesla shows a generic media widget (site name, prev/stop/next) without Media Session metadata. Without handlers, the hardware buttons did not drive the page's own queue. Whether the buttons call navigator.mediaSession handlers is not documented.

Under Chromium's autoplay policy, an AudioContext created before a user gesture starts 'suspended' and needs resume() after a tap. A Tesla-browser project confirms the browser may refuse audio until the first tap. The PWA-install exemption does not apply because there is no install path in the car.

AudioWorklet has been in Chromium since Chrome 66 and needs a secure context (HTTPS). Every current Tesla Chromium (136–148) is newer than that. No published in-car test of AudioWorklet was found. A Web-Audio streaming player (Music Assistant) had buffer-underrun-like glitches in the Tesla browser in Dec 2025, fixed in a later app release (Apr 2026).

SharedArrayBuffer needs HTTPS plus cross-origin isolation (COOP: same-origin, COEP: require-corp or credentialless); it shipped in desktop Chrome 92. No Tesla-specific confirmation exists, and one probe says the build is QtWebEngine with some APIs compiled out. Treat it as unverified.

An in-car probe (Oct 2026, car and firmware not stated) reports the browser as QtWebEngine (embedded Chromium). Available: WebSocket, Canvas2D, WebGL, createImageBitmap, WebAssembly. MSE codecs limited. Not available: WebCodecs, WebRTC; getUserMedia blocked at compile time. This conflicts with 2026.26 camera/mic support on AMD, so APIs differ by hardware and firmware.

navigator.geolocation works over HTTPS with a permission prompt. Support goes back to firmware 5.9 but has broken and been fixed several times, e.g. instant 'User denied Geolocation' on 2020.16 Chromium 79 and a fix in 2022.4.5. Current 2026 Tesla web apps rely on it.
The car's GPS reaches the browser about once per second (1 Hz). At 120 km/h that is a 33 m jump per fix, so apps interpolate between fixes.

On newer (AMD) cars the browser gets the car's own fused position (wheels + steering + satellites, the same one the native map uses). It keeps updating as 'Position estimated' when satellite fix is lost (tunnels), and coords.speed carries the car's own speed. On older Intel (pre-2022) cars, coords.speed is zero or absent even while moving and updates stop when the fix drops, so speed must come from position deltas and parked GPS jitter must be filtered.

Tesla web-app developers report watchPosition crashing the Tesla Chromium tab on highway drives, plus DeviceOrientation sensors crashing it. They poll getCurrentPosition every 2–4 s instead (tesla-cloud 2 s; teslaradar 4 s with maximumAge ≤3 s). Both read coords.speed directly.
No published figures exist for geolocation latency (fix age vs real position) in the browser. The 'several seconds lag' reports concern the Tesla owner/Fleet API, not browser geolocation.

The browser reloads mid-drive in the field, so web apps must restore state after reload. Memory pressure is a known problem on Intel MCU2: decoded bitmaps not freed, the ad blocker pitched as a fix for memory filling up. Developers cap pixel ratio at 1× and cache sizes.
The car has no speechSynthesis voices installed, so the browser's built-in TTS is unusable.

2026.32 added an optional built-in ad blocker (AD button). When on, it blocks ad trackers, third-party analytics scripts and heavy banner animations at the network-request level, with no per-site allowlist.

localStorage persists across sessions in practice: Tesla apps store last GPS fix and preferences there. The owner can wipe all browser data via Controls > Service > Clear Browser Data. Since 2026.26, bookmarks sync across the owner's cars via the Tesla profile.

There is no app or PWA install path in the car ('You can't install apps on a Tesla'); users save a Favorite or bookmark. No in-car confirmation was found that Service Worker or Cache Storage works. Known Tesla-targeted production apps checked (codriver, teslas.cloud, teslabrowserapps) serve no service worker, and teslaradar explicitly ships no offline service worker.
The browser needs a data connection. Standard Connectivity cars get it only over Wi-Fi or a mobile hotspot; Premium Connectivity adds cellular. Coverage gaps and tunnels drop connectivity mid-drive.

The Fullscreen API is unconfirmed for arbitrary sites. 2026.26 makes the browser go full-screen automatically for certain streaming sites (HBO Max, Prime Video, ...) and only while parked. While driving, the browser window is explicitly not full-screen.
2026.26 lets sites request the cabin camera and microphone (per-request prompt). Camera works parked only, and only on AMD Ryzen cars.
Since 2026.20 owners can block the Web Browser (and Theater and Arcade) with PIN-protected Parental Controls (Controls > Safety > Parental Controls).

Tesla's official position: there are no published developer terms or programme for third-party in-browser web apps. The manual tells drivers to avoid using the touchscreen while in motion and not to read or send texts while moving. Tesla is nonetheless actively building out the browser (bookmark sync, camera/mic, ad blocker).

The external speaker (Pedestrian Warning System) is car-controlled. It emits PWS sound below about 40 km/h and in reverse, and Boombox external playback is allowed only in Park. Browser audio goes to the cabin speakers, so Tesbox's 'exterior perspective' can only be simulated in-cabin.
Audio settings include a subwoofer slider in Tone and 'Immersive Sound' on premium-audio cars. The car applies the user's EQ to all media including browser audio, presumably.

Chrome throttles timers in hidden pages to 1 s, and to 1 min after 5 min hidden and silent. Pages that made sound in the last 30 s are exempt. If the minimised Tesla browser counts as hidden, main-thread physics loops would be throttled while the audio thread keeps running.
Prior art: MIT-licensed open-source engine-sound projects already target the Tesla browser (GPS speed and acceleration into procedural Web Audio).

Sources: teslaoracle.com 2022-05-11; notateslaapp news 760; videocardz (via search summary only, not fetched).
recommendations: Assume browser audio becomes the car's active media source. Tesbox will pause the user's Spotify or radio rather than mix with it. Say so in onboarding.
Require a 'Start engine' tap before creating or resuming the AudioContext. After any page reload mid-drive, show one large tap-to-resume control, because audio cannot restart without a gesture.

Use an AudioWorklet synth served over HTTPS, and keep a ScriptProcessor or plain-node fallback. Do not depend on SharedArrayBuffer: send control parameters (rpm, load, gear) over the worklet MessagePort at 30–60 Hz. Only enable COOP/COEP if an in-car probe shows crossOriginIsolated === true.

Do the speed/RPM physics and smoothing inside the AudioWorklet or behind a fixed-rate interpolator. GPS arrives at only ~1 Hz, and main-thread timers may be throttled if the minimised browser counts as hidden.

Speed input: poll getCurrentPosition every ~1 s with maximumAge 0–1000 rather than watchPosition, since watchPosition reportedly crashes the tab. Use coords.speed when it is non-null and non-zero (AMD). Otherwise derive speed from haversine distance over time with outlier rejection and a stopped-hysteresis filter (Intel). Interpolate and extrapolate between 1 Hz fixes for smooth RPM.
Expect GPS dropouts on Intel cars (tunnels). Hold the last speed and decay toward it, or freeze RPM, rather than snapping to idle. On AMD, keep consuming the car's dead-reckoned fixes.
Estimating load from GPS acceleration at 1 Hz is coarse. Smooth with a short filter, use a lag-tolerant blend, and let the selected Tesla model's mass and power scale the load.

Identify the car from the user's model choice plus a WebGL UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL check (AMD vs Intel) and screen.width/height × devicePixelRatio. Do not rely on a 'Tesla/' UA token, which was removed in 2026.26.

Lay out for the in-motion viewport: about 773×601 CSS px on Model 3/Y at dpr 1.53, and 804×638 on Juniper at dpr 1.96. Handle resize events when shifting P→D. Size touch targets in physical pixels (×dpr) and keep the downshift button reachable.
Account for Tesla's speed-dependent volume. Do not also raise synth loudness with road speed by default, or offer an 'auto gain' toggle. Duck the synth's own level at standstill.

Build a probe page and test it in the car before committing to the steering-wheel shift design. The probe should check: AudioWorklet, crossOriginIsolated, serviceWorker registration and Cache Storage, requestFullscreen, Media Session action handlers firing from left-scroll press and tilt, document.visibilityState when minimised, and coords.speed/accuracy/timestamp cadence.

For scroll-wheel shifting, try a muted or silent HTMLAudioElement (or a MediaStreamDestination routed to <audio>) to register a media session. Bind navigator.mediaSession 'nexttrack' to upshift and 'previoustrack' to downshift, rather than 'play'/'pause' toggles. Tilt is a more natural shift gesture than press, and Tesla may pause the media element itself.

Offline: ship one small precached bundle with no runtime CDN or third-party analytics. The 2026.32 ad blocker can strip third-party scripts, and connectivity drops in tunnels. Register a service worker opportunistically, keep everything in memory after first load so the session survives connectivity loss, and persist settings in localStorage wrapped in try/catch, which the user can wipe.
Keep memory and GPU light for Intel MCU2: canvas at 1× backing store, no large decoded images, minimal DOM churn, and a visual frame rate capped at about 30 fps on Intel.
Implement 'exterior perspective' as in-cabin filtering (distance and occlusion EQ). The browser cannot drive the external PWS/Boombox speaker, and Boombox is Park-only.
Design the driving UI for zero typing and minimal glances, with a passenger-oriented disclaimer. Tesla publishes no third-party web-app terms, and owners can block the browser via parental controls.
openQuestions: The exact UA string on 2026.26+ firmware (Chromium 148) for Intel and AMD cars, and whether navigator.userAgentData or Client Hints expose anything useful.

Do the steering-wheel left-scroll press, tilt-left and tilt-right reach navigator.mediaSession action handlers in the Tesla browser? Does Tesla pause the HTMLMediaElement directly instead, and does a Web-Audio-only page, with no media element, register as 'browser audio' in the Miniplayer at all?
Does an AudioContext keep rendering when the browser is minimised to the Miniplayer, and is document.visibilityState 'hidden' then (which would mean timer throttling)?

Are AudioWorklet, SharedArrayBuffer (crossOriginIsolated), Service Worker or Cache Storage, and the Fullscreen API enabled in Tesla's Chromium build, on both Intel and AMD? One probe reports some APIs compiled out (WebCodecs, WebRTC).
Geolocation latency: how old is each fix when delivered, and is coords.speed filtered or lagged relative to the speedometer? What are the coords.accuracy values in practice?
Is watchPosition still crashing on Chromium 148 (2026.26+), or was that specific to older or Intel builds? Only one AI-agent-authored repo reports it.
Audio output latency and glitch behaviour of Web Audio on Intel MCU2 (needed latencyHint and buffer size); the Dec 2025 Music Assistant underrun report hints at problems.
Which Tesla trims lack a subwoofer or premium audio in 2025–2026 (e.g. Model 3/Y Standard or RWD variants)? Does the user's Tone/subwoofer EQ apply to browser audio?
Is the browser restricted while driving in any region, and does Tesla limit browser interaction above certain speeds?
Does the browser page survive car sleep or wake and drive cycles (persist vs reload), and does localStorage survive firmware updates?
The conflicting S/X 2021+ devicePixelRatio after 2026.26 (1.56 vs unscaled), and Cybertruck viewport values.
Does Tesla's own speed-dependent volume compensation apply to browser audio exactly as to native media, and can it be measured?

verdicts.claim: 1a. Tesla's in-car browser is Chromium-based and was moved from Chromium 136 to 140 on S, 3, X, Y and Cybertruck in the 2026.14 branch (2026.14.3 dated 2026-04-28; 2026.14.6 dated 2026-05-12).
verdicts.evidence: NotATeslaApp lists 'Chromium Browser Updated: The browser was updated to version 140, up from version 136', Models S/3/X/Y/CT, with no Intel or AMD restriction. The same entry is on 2026.14 (Apr 15, 2026), 2026.14.1 (Apr 17), 2026.14.2 (Apr 22), 2026.14.3 (Apr 28) and 2026.14.6 (May 12). So Chromium 140 first shipped in 2026.14 on Apr 15, 2026, not in 2026.14.3. Medium-high confidence: no Tesla primary source exists, only NotATeslaApp's observation.

verdicts.claim: 1b. The Chromium 140 change has Tesla release-note wording saying it 'improves WebGPU performance' (and the summary's 'Only WebGPU is backed by Tesla's own wording').
verdicts.evidence: NotATeslaApp files 'Chromium Browser Updated' under 'Undocumented Change', meaning it is not in Tesla's release notes. The sentence 'increases compatibility with modern web standards, improves WebGPU performance, and resolves known issues' is NotATeslaApp's own editorial text. Tesla published nothing about this browser change, WebGPU included.

verdicts.claim: 2. The 2026.26 Summer Update moved the browser to Chromium 148 (third-party measurement; Tesla's notes give no number).
verdicts.evidence: codriver's guide says 'the browser moved to a Chromium 148 engine'. Its changelog entry of 10 Aug 2026 says 'The summer-2026 firmware (Chromium 148) changed the browser's pixel density'. keylimesoda/tesla-iptv cites a separate in-car measurement by the cliamp-web author on a 2026 MY Performance ('804x638 CSS @ dpr 1.96, Chrome 148'). NotATeslaApp's 2026.26 page has no Chromium number. Dates: 2026.26 is dated July 26, 2026; 2026.26.6 Aug 11; 2026.26.200 Sep 2; 2026.26.300 Sep 14. Medium confidence: these are vendor and hobbyist reports, and the cliamp-web measurement can only be seen second-hand in tesla-iptv.

verdicts.claim: 3. Historical UAs carried a Tesla/<firmware> token (e.g. Chromium/88 ... Tesla/2021.36.5.5-c6d521764ab9; Linux x86_64 ... Chrome/100 ... Tesla/feature-2022.20.9-31-abc). None identified the model or MCU; Intel and AMD both report x86_64.
verdicts.evidence: user-agents.net and useragents.io list the exact Chromium/88.0.4324.150 ... Tesla/2021.36.5.5-c6d521764ab9 string, plus Chromium 75 (2019), 79 (2020) and Tesla/DEV-BUILD-<hash> variants, all as 'X11; GNU/Linux' with no model or MCU field. trunc.org gives the Chrome/100 'X11; Linux x86_64 ... Tesla/feature-2022.20.9-31-abc' string; its 'abc' suffix looks like a placeholder or redaction. Pre-Chromium MCU1 cars sent 'QtCarBrowser' WebKit UAs. Caveat: no source shows an AMD-car UA next to an Intel one, so 'both report x86_64' is inferred (both are x86-64 CPUs), not observed.

verdicts.claim: 4. 2026.26 removed the 'Tesla' marker from the UA and changed the reported screen size; developers now detect the car from physical screen size and the WebGL renderer; tesla-cloud saw UA changes across releases and mobile-like presentation.
verdicts.evidence: codriver's changelog (10 Aug 2026) says: 'The update also dropped the Tesla marker the browser used to send and changed the reported screen size ... Detection now works off the physical screen size and the in-car graphics chip.' That is the only source for the removal. tesla-cloud's device.js does say 'The in-car browser has been observed presenting itself as mobile, and Tesla has changed the UA across releases'. But tesla-cloud does not confirm the removal: it still matches /Tesla\// and /TESLA_AUTO/, and its PR #435 test matrix includes a 'Tesla 2026.26 (UA token)' profile. That matrix was run in headless Chromium and the PR calls its band 'inferred rather than measured', not taken in a car. The claim is plausible but rests on one vendor.

verdicts.claim: 5. 2026.26 turned on a browser-wide default page zoom: on Model 3/Y dpr 1.0 -> ~1.53, CSS viewport ~1920x1160 -> ~1254x784 (parked); no user zoom control.
verdicts.evidence: NotATeslaApp's undocumented change 'Web Browser Zoom' (Models S/3/X/Y/CT, no hardware tag) says 'The browser zoom level has been increased ... you can't manually adjust the zoom level' and notes some sites switch to tablet or mobile layouts. Four sources agree on 1.53 for 1920x1200 cars: codriver ('a Model 3 or Y has its browser enlarge everything by half again'), tesla-cloud (dpr 1.53), sedicivalvole (photographed 'screen 1254 x 784, DPR 1.53') and tesla-iptv. Correction: 1254x784 is the screen size (1920x1200/1.53). The page viewport that matches the old 1920x1160 is about 1255x758 per tesla-cloud PR #435. The 'no pinch' part is not verified. The zoom factor differs by panel: about 1.96 on 2560x1440 screens, and S/X 2021+ is either unscaled (codriver) or 1.56 (tesla-iptv).

verdicts.claim: 6. Browser is not full-screen while driving: 3/Y 2020-25 ~773x601 CSS @1.53 in motion (1254x784 parked); 'new Model Y (Juniper, 16-inch 2560x1440)' 804x638 @1.96 in motion (~1306x735 parked); S/X conflict (1410x833 @1.56 vs unscaled).
verdicts.evidence: The 3/Y figure has independent support. sedicivalvole reports 'photographed Tesla split-view evidence at 773 x 601, screen 1254 x 784, DPR 1.53' and describes the app 'while driving - 773 x 601 CSS px beside the vehicle view'. tesla-navidrome was tuned for a ~1170x920 px browser area before the zoom change (~1183x920 device px), which is consistent. Caveats: sedicivalvole calls this the split view next to the vehicle visualisation, so it is a layout state and may not be strictly tied to motion. The 804x638 @1.96 figure is relayed second-hand by tesla-iptv, a repo created 2026-10-03 with 0 stars and no licence; the original measurement cannot be checked. 'Juniper, 16-inch' is wrong: the standard Juniper Model Y has a 15.4-inch screen; 16-inch 2560x1440 is on the Model Y Performance and Model Y L, and since about Oct 2026 on every North American Model 3. The S/X conflict stands: codriver (27 Aug 2026) says S/X 'hands the browser its whole screen unscaled'.

verdicts.claim: 7. Hardware is told apart by GPU/performance, not UA. Intel Atom MCU2 is in pre-Dec-2021 3/Y and 2018-2021 S/X; AMD Ryzen MCU3 is in 3/Y from ~Dec 2021, refresh S/X and Cybertruck. Camera/mic in 2026.26 is AMD-only.
verdicts.evidence: TeslaOracle (May 2022): AMD Ryzen APU in Model 3/Y from December 2021 and in refresh S/X from production start. NotATeslaApp (Apr 2022): MCU2 from spring 2018 for S/X and fall 2017 for Model 3, and MCU2 cannot be upgraded to MCU3. Wikipedia: S/X moved Tegra -> Intel Atom around 2018 and to AMD Ryzen with the Palladium refresh. NotATeslaApp tags the 2026.26 'Web Browser' camera/mic feature 'AMD' with 'Camera is only available while parked'; codriver agrees (parked only, AMD only). codriver detects hardware from the graphics chip. Caveats: the Ryzen switch was gradual and varied by factory and market (late 2021 for Shanghai-built MY). Pre-2018 S/X upgraded from MCU1 to MCU2 also run Intel Atom. No fetched source covers the Cybertruck CPU directly.

verdicts.claim: 8. WebGL performance (Aug 2026): a 2023 Model Y (AMD) holds 60 fps for a custom WebGL 3D map; a 2019 Model 3 / 2017 Model S (Intel) gets 10-15 fps with a general-purpose map engine and 25-35 fps with a purpose-built renderer.
verdicts.evidence: codriver changelog (22-23 Aug 2026, 'Peregrine' renderer): 'On a 2019 Model 3, the pre-2022 Intel computer, Peregrine draws the full 3D map at 25 to 35 frames a second, where the ordinary flat map on that same car manages 10 to 15 ... It holds a steady 60 on a 2023 Model Y, and we proved it on a 2017 Model S as well.' The earlier general-purpose 3D views managed 'about 10 fps' (guide). Caveats: these are a commercial vendor's own numbers. The 10-15 fps figure is the 2D flat map on the 2019 Model 3 only. A 2017 Model S shipped with MCU1 (Tegra), so the test car must have had the MCU2 retrofit.

verdicts.claim: 9. Browser audio keeps playing in Drive or in motion; only the picture of a <video> element is suppressed; canvas/WebGL drawing is not suppressed.
verdicts.evidence: tesla-video-drive: '<video> elements are paused immediately in Drive (last frame frozen, audio continues)'. It uses '<audio> MP3 ... (Tesla doesn't block audio)' and a JSMpeg WebGL canvas at 30 fps while driving. tesla-iptv: suppression 'does not apply to <canvas>'. The Music Assistant OP: 'chromium-based web browser that can play audio during vehicle in drive'. sedicivalvole runs GPS-driven audio in cabin drive tests. codriver's WebGL map runs while driving. The two video repos disagree on one point: tesla-video-drive says Tesla calls video.pause() and drawImage(video) gives a black frame, while tesla-iptv says an off-screen video keeps decoding and can be copied to a canvas. This does not affect pure Web Audio plus canvas. All of these are hobbyist reports; there is no Tesla documentation.

verdicts.claim: 10. Owner's manual: browser audio continues when the browser is minimised, can be paused or played from the Miniplayer, and other media resumes after browser audio pauses or ends. So browser audio replaces the user's media rather than mixing with it.
verdicts.evidence: Model 3 manual (tesla.cn en_cn copy): 'When you play audio through the web browser and then minimize the browser, Model 3 continues the browser audio in the background. You can pause or play the browser audio through the media Miniplayer. If there was media playing before the browser audio began, the media resumes after you pause or end browser audio.' 'No mixing or ducking' is an inference from the resume wording; it is reasonable but not stated outright. The tesla.com US copy returned 403 to the fetcher.

verdicts.claim: 11. Owner's manual: volume 'may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings'; volume may drop briefly when shifting into Reverse.
verdicts.evidence: Same manual page, verbatim: 'Volume may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings.' and 'Note Audio volume may temporarily lower when you shift into Reverse.' Scroll-wheel roll 'adjusts the volume for media, voice commands, and phone calls.'

verdicts.claim: 12. Left scroll button: press = play/pause media, tilt = prev/next, roll = volume, long press = custom shortcut, both = gear selector/restart. An <audio> page gets a generic widget (site name, prev/stop/next) with no metadata. Whether the buttons call navigator.mediaSession handlers is undocumented.
verdicts.evidence: Model 3 manual, Steering Wheel page: Normal mode Press = 'Play/pause media', Tilt left/right = 'Next/previous track', Scroll = 'Adjust volume'. Long press = 'Activate/set function' (Controls > Display > Scroll Button Function). 'Press both briefly' = 'Activate secondary drive mode selector (P, R, N, D)'; 'Press both and hold' = 'Restart the touchscreen'. fuse-riders #135 (2026-09-15): the Tesla widget reads 'Fuse Riders / andeplane.github.io with generic previous / stop / next buttons', and the buttons 'do not drive the radio's own queue'. The issue was closed with no in-car result recorded. tesla-navidrome lists 'scroll wheel next/back' as still needing vehicle testing. sedicivalvole marks its Tesla Media Session test 'TESLA MEDIA SESSION PENDING'. Media Session routing therefore remains unverified everywhere.

verdicts.claim: 13. Chromium autoplay policy: an AudioContext created before a gesture starts 'suspended' and needs resume() after a tap. A Tesla project confirms the first-tap requirement. The PWA-install exemption doesn't apply (no install path).
verdicts.evidence: Chrome autoplay doc: 'If an AudioContext is created before the document receives a user gesture, it will be created in the "suspended" state, and you will need to call resume() after the user gesture.' tesla-video-drive: 'the browser may refuse audio until the first tap'. teslabrowserapps.com: 'You can't install apps on a Tesla'. Missed: the policy has a third desktop exemption, the Media Engagement Index (MEI). Whether Tesla's build applies MEI is unknown, so design for a tap regardless.

verdicts.claim: 14a. AudioWorklet has been in Chromium since Chrome 66 and needs a secure context (HTTPS).
verdicts.evidence: MDN browser-compat-data api/AudioWorklet.json and AudioWorkletNode.json: chrome version_added '66'. MDN: 'Secure context required'. Caveat: Tesla's Chromium build is known to strip APIs (see 'missed'), so the engine version does not guarantee the feature.

verdicts.claim: 14b. No published in-car test of AudioWorklet was found.
verdicts.evidence: sedicivalvole (public GitHub, PolyForm Noncommercial) is a GPS speed-reactive music and engine-sound app for the Tesla browser. It uses 'a production AudioWorklet score' (FRACTURE) and worklet effects. It records in-cabin drive tests: R4-04 PARTIAL PASS on 2026-08-31, with UNDERWATER confirmed during braking in an active drive test, and owner listening 'inside Tesla to build 20260908-0807'. A failed build 'stuttered' in-car on streamed tracks. No source gives an isolated pass/fail for AudioWorklet itself, but an AudioWorklet-based graph has been reported running in a Tesla.

verdicts.claim: 14c. A Web-Audio streaming player (Music Assistant) had buffer-underrun-like glitches in the Tesla browser in Dec 2025, fixed in a later app release (Apr 2026).
verdicts.evidence: Discussion #4563 (Dec 18, 2025) reports playback that is 'slow and sounds like buffer underruns', with Plex Web working smoothly. The OP's only follow-up (Apr 24, 2026) is 'It works smoothly in 2.8.6'. The thread never says the player uses Web Audio and names no cause or fix. The April 2026 timing also matches Tesla's Chromium 136->140 rollout (2026.14, Apr 15), so the fix may have come from Tesla's firmware rather than the app.

corrections: Chromium 140 first shipped in 2026.14 (Apr 15, 2026) and appears in every 2026.14.x release. 2026.14.3 (Apr 28) and 2026.14.6 (May 12) are later point releases, not the introduction.

NotATeslaApp marks the Chromium 136->140 change as an 'Undocumented Change'. The 'improves WebGPU performance' wording is NotATeslaApp's, not Tesla's. The summary's 'Only WebGPU is backed by Tesla's own wording' is false: Tesla has published no browser-engine wording.
2026.26 is dated July 26, 2026 (2026.26.6 Aug 11; 2026.26.200 Sep 2; 2026.26.300 Sep 14). The newest listed release is 2026.38 (Sep 30, 2026), with no browser changes noted.

1254x784 is the CSS screen size (1920x1200 / 1.53). The parked page viewport that corresponds to the old 1920x1160 is about 1255x758 (tesla-cloud PR #435). Do not mix screen.* and innerWidth/innerHeight figures.

The 16-inch 2560x1440 panel (dpr ~1.96 after 2026.26) is not the standard Juniper Model Y, which has 15.4 inches. It is on the Model Y Performance and Model Y L, and since ~Oct 2026 on every North American Model 3 trim. Never hard-code 1.53; read devicePixelRatio at runtime.

The 773x601 window is described by sedicivalvole as the split view beside the vehicle visualisation. It may be a layout state as well as a motion restriction. Handle resize events and do not assume one fixed in-motion size.
The 'Tesla UA marker removed in 2026.26' rests on one source (codriver). tesla-cloud still matches Tesla/ and TESLA_AUTO tokens and never measured removal in a car.

Codriver's fps figures: 10-15 fps is the 2D flat map on a 2019 Model 3. The old general-purpose 3D map was ~10 fps. The 2017 Model S test car must have had the MCU2 retrofit, since 2017 S shipped with MCU1 Tegra.
Music Assistant #4563 does not say the player used Web Audio or what fixed it. It only says it 'works smoothly in 2.8.6' (Apr 24, 2026), which coincides with the Chromium 140 firmware rollout.

An in-car AudioWorklet-based audio graph has been reported: sedicivalvole cabin drive tests, Aug 31 and Sep 8, 2026. 'No published in-car test' is therefore too strong, although no isolated compatibility pass/fail exists.
Chrome's autoplay policy also has a desktop Media Engagement Index exemption. Whether Tesla's build honours it is unknown, so keep the tap-to-start flow.

Manual wording: tilt left/right = 'Next/previous track'. Long press = customisable 'Multifunction'. 'Press both briefly' = secondary drive-mode selector (P/R/N/D), relevant to stalkless cars. 'Press both and hold' = restart touchscreen.
missed: A design risk for Tesbox: the left scroll button press is documented as 'Play/pause media', and browser audio is a media source controlled from the Miniplayer. Using a scroll-wheel press for upshift will probably pause or toggle Tesbox's audio at the OS level. Whether the press reaches the page as a key event or a mediaSession 'pause' action is unverified (fuse-riders #135, tesla-navidrome and sedicivalvole all list it as untested or pending). Tilt left/right (next/previous track) is a candidate for up/down shift via mediaSession handlers, but that is also unverified. Sources: https://www.tesla.cn/ownersmanual/model3/en_cn/GUID-DEB259CC-ABAC-4BFC-8D10-B7B1BBCFCB1F.html, https://github.com/andeplane/fuse-riders/issues/135

Tesla's Chromium build strips APIs, so the version number does not tell you what is available. The tesla-video-drive probe reports 'WebCodecs Not available', 'WebRTC Not available', 'getUserMedia Blocked (compile-time)' and 'MediaSource Limited codecs'. Its firmware and hardware are unstated and it likely predates 2026.26. It describes the browser as QtWebEngine (embedded Chromium); this is unverified. Tesbox must feature-detect AudioWorklet, SharedArrayBuffer, Service Worker and Fullscreen and include fallbacks (e.g. AudioBufferSourceNode/ScriptProcessor). Source: https://github.com/Dailroy/tesla-video-drive

2026.26 camera access is parked-only and AMD-only. Sites must request permission ('Tap to grant permissions when a website requests access'). Source: https://www.notateslaapp.com/software-updates/version/2026.26/release-notes

2026.20 (May 30, 2026) added Parental Controls that can block Browser, Theater and Arcade (Controls > Safety > Parental Controls, in Park). Source: https://www.notateslaapp.com/software-updates/version/2026.20/release-notes
2026.26 also added browser bookmark sync across the owner's vehicles, useful for 'add Tesbox once'. Source: https://www.notateslaapp.com/software-updates/version/2026.26/release-notes

MCU1 cars (pre-2018 S/X without the MCU2 retrofit) ran an old WebKit 'QtCarBrowser' (UA e.g. 'AppleWebKit/601.1 ... Tesla QtCarBrowser'). They cannot run Tesbox and should get a clear unsupported message. Source: https://useragents.io/explore/browsers/types/browser/maker/tesla-motors-029

Prior art (do not reuse code; read only for public facts). sedicivalvole (github.com/enuzzo/sedicivalvole, PolyForm Noncommercial) is a GPS speed-reactive engine-sound and music Drive Lab for the Tesla browser. It uses AudioWorklet, computes RPM from real gear ratios and tyre size, and logs in-cabin listening. Its design surface is 773x601 CSS. Antonio-R1/engine-sound-generator (MIT, Web Audio/AudioWorklet engine sound, last pushed 2022) is generic prior art.

Clean-room flag: github.com/UnendlessGit/juniper-sound-lab (an 'engine-sound simulator for the Tesla browser', created 2026-10-04) mentions rupteur in its README. I did not read it, and Tesbox research should avoid it.

Other post-2026.26 environment reports (tesla-iptv, low confidence): CSS media queries now report pointer: fine and hover: hover, so do not rely on them for touch detection. maxTouchPoints is still 16. prefers-color-scheme reports light. The canvas backing store is capped at 2x device pixels. Source: https://github.com/keylimesoda/tesla-iptv

codriver: the car's GPS reports once a second, the reported speed is 'the car's own number' (dead-reckoned position), and older Intel cars 'go quiet when the fix drops'. Tesbox should interpolate between 1 Hz fixes and handle fix loss on Intel. Source: https://codriver.io/changelog

sedicivalvole recorded an in-car audio stutter on a streamed-track build (20260903-1752) despite a 54 Mbps speed test. Network-fed audio is fragile in the car; a fully procedural, offline synth avoids this. Source: https://github.com/enuzzo/sedicivalvole/blob/main/docs/TESLA-TEST-QUEUE-2026-08-31.md

The browser is reachable both parked and in Drive; teslabrowserapps.com says 'Media plays while parked, per Tesla's browser rules'. That is ambiguous and likely refers to video, but it shows sites still describe the driving rules inconsistently. Source: https://www.teslabrowserapps.com/

research.summary:
Short answer: no public evidence shows that the steering-wheel scroll wheels reach a web page in the Tesla browser. Tesla's manuals route the left wheel (press, tilt, roll) to the car's own media player and volume, and the right wheel to Autopilot. No Tesla document mentions keyboard, wheel or Gamepad events from those wheels. One other GPS engine-sound web app (Rombo) says in its FAQ that "the car keeps those buttons for its own media player and doesn't pass them on to web pages". The only plausible path is the Media Session API. Pages playing an <audio> element do appear in Tesla's media widget, which has prev/stop/next buttons. Whether a wheel tilt fires the page's nexttrack/previoustrack handlers has not been tested by anyone. Pressing the wheel probably pauses or mutes the page audio at platform level, and getting audio back often needs a tap. Manual upshift by scroll-wheel press is therefore unproven and risky. It should be an experimental, self-tested option, and touchscreen shifting should be the main control.

The Gamepad API works in the Tesla browser with Bluetooth controllers (best with PS5 DualSense; 2023.26 added Bluetooth pairing). Controllers can show up with a "TESLA VIRTUAL GAMEPAD" ID. Bluetooth keyboards and mice do not work. As of the 2026.26 update the browser reportedly runs Chromium 148 (third-party claim) with devicePixelRatio 1.53. AudioWorklet works there. The browser stays usable in Drive but full screen is blocked while moving, the browser hides in reverse, and the main thread can freeze for 100-300 ms (seconds during modem outages). Browser GPS updates about once a second.

Live pedal, speed or gear data from the car is not realistic for live sound. The Fleet API vehicle_data endpoint allows 60 requests/min and costs $1 per 500 requests, about $7.20 per hour at 1 Hz. Fleet Telemetry sends data in 500 ms buckets. VehicleSpeed and Gear can stream every 1 s, but PedalPosition and motor speed/torque only every 10 s (Teslemetry's limits). Setup needs a server, a domain key, mTLS, OAuth and pairing a virtual key. The unofficial Owner API is being shut down. Use GPS plus prediction in the AudioWorklet.

claims.claim: Model 3 (2026 manual, stalkless Highland): left scroll wheel in Normal mode: press = play/pause media, tilt left/right = next/previous track, scroll up/down = volume. Long press = a customisable function (Controls > Display > Scroll Wheel Function). Tilt in a call = answer/decline. Pressing both wheels briefly opens the secondary P/R/N/D selector; holding both restarts the touchscreen. Right wheel = Self-Driving (press activates Autosteer/FSD, tilt = follow distance, scroll = max speed).

Model Y manual (Dec 2024 snapshot, before Juniper): pressing the left scroll button mutes/unmutes, rolling it changes volume, pushing it right/left goes to the next/previous song, station or Favorite. Pressing the right scroll button starts a voice command. So what a 'press' does differs by model and year (mute vs play/pause).

Model S/X 2021+ yoke or wheel: pushing the left scroll button left/right = previous/next song or station, rolling = volume, pressing = mute or pause/play. Long press opens a customisation menu on the instrument cluster. Right scroll button = Autopilot. The manual says 'There is currently no action associated with pushing the right scroll button to the left and right.' Some yoke controls are capacitive buttons.

No Tesla documentation says that steering-wheel scroll-wheel input reaches web content as keyboard events, wheel events, Gamepad input or Media Session actions. Every documented function is a car-level function (media player, volume, mirrors, Autopilot).

Rombo, another GPS engine-sound web app for the Tesla browser, says in its FAQ: 'Can I shift gears with the steering-wheel buttons? Not for now. The car keeps those buttons for its own media player and doesn't pass them on to web pages.'
The tesla-pi project (CarPlay/RetroArch streamed into the Tesla browser) says 'Steering-wheel controls are not supported. The Tesla's scroll wheels/buttons have no path back to CarPlay.'

When a page plays audio through an <audio> element, the Tesla browser shows a media widget for it. Without Media Session metadata the widget shows the page name and origin with generic previous/stop/next buttons (reporter's in-car photo, Sept 2026). Nobody has confirmed whether those buttons or the steering wheel fire the page's Media Session handlers in a Tesla; the PR that implemented the handlers lists the Tesla check as 'Not testable here'.

Owner's manual (Model Y): when you minimise the browser, its audio keeps playing in the background, and the media Miniplayer can pause/play it. If other media was playing before, it resumes when the browser audio is paused or ends. The steering-wheel tilt does next/previous for media. Volume 'may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings'.

The car can pause the browser's audio when the user changes music or takes a call, and the page then needs a tap to resume. One field log (2026-07-19) shows programmatic AudioContext.resume() retried repeatedly and refused until a user gesture. A Tesla-specific fix keeps an inaudible oscillator running so the AudioContext stays alive.

In Chrome, the Media Session API routes hardware media keys to page action handlers (play, pause, stop, previoustrack, nexttrack, seek*). A media notification appears only for media with 'full' audio focus that lasts at least 5 s; the article only describes HTMLMediaElement triggering it, so Web Audio-only output may not create a media session.

Activation-triggering events (needed to resume an AudioContext) are trusted keydown, mousedown, pointerdown only for mouse, pointerup for touch/pen, and touchend. A touch pointerdown does not unlock audio, and neither do Gamepad input or Media Session actions (they are not on the list).

Tesla 2023.26 added Bluetooth game controllers ('Use Bluetooth controllers to play games in Arcade... works best with PS5 controllers'). The manual says up to two Bluetooth devices at a time (e.g. one phone plus one controller). USB controllers need the glovebox port on cars built after about Nov 2021.

The Gamepad API works in the Tesla browser with USB and Bluetooth controllers. Tesla can present controllers with the ID 'TESLA VIRTUAL GAMEPAD' and mapping='standard', but maps Nintendo controllers by label instead of position (A/B and X/Y swapped). getGamepads() can stall the main thread for more than 20 ms on Tesla's Bluetooth HID stack; that project also disabled rumble because of stalls.

Gamepad spec: getGamepads() returns an empty list until a gamepad user gesture (a button press or a large stick movement) has been seen. The API is polled; there are no per-button events, only gamepadconnected and gamepaddisconnected.

Keyboard and mouse input do not work natively in the Tesla browser; Tesla's Bluetooth accepts only phones and game controllers, not HID keyboards. Cheap Bluetooth 'media remotes' or keyboard-type paddles that act as HID keyboards are not a viable input.

Native Arcade games can use the steering-wheel buttons ('You may need to use the steering wheel buttons or a Bluetooth or USB controller'). Beach Buggy Racing 2 (2019) used the real steering wheel and brake pedal in Park only. These inputs are available to native apps; there is no documented route to the browser.

The browser keeps working in Drive. One project 'Works while parked, charging and in D mode' and plays audio while driving. Full screen is not allowed while moving, and the browser disappears in Reverse. A web page cannot change either behaviour.

The 2026.26 update (summer 2026) raised the browser's default zoom (devicePixelRatio 1.0 to 1.53; about 1255x773 CSS px against the old 1920x1183), added cabin camera and mic access (parked only, AMD Ryzen cars), and synced bookmarks. A third party says it also moved the engine to Chromium 148. Tesla's UA has changed between releases (tokens include 'Tesla/' and, on some builds, 'TESLA_AUTO'), so UA sniffing is fragile.

AudioWorklet works in the Tesla browser over HTTPS. The browser's main thread stalls for 100-300 ms on cellular micro-outages and for several seconds (3.3-16.3 s seen) during modem recovery, so audio should be generated on the audio thread. The browser has no devtools.
The Tesla browser blocks requests to raw IP addresses and local network ranges, so in-car testing needs a real domain (ideally HTTPS, which AudioWorklet also requires).

Browser geolocation in the Tesla updates about once a second, so GPS speed lags the dashboard speedometer. Two independent GPS engine-sound apps say this. One probe tool also says geolocation is 'often blocked at the car level' and that CAN data (pedal, RPM, true wheel speed) is not available to web content.

Fleet API rate limits per device per account: Realtime Data (vehicle_data) 60 requests/min, Device Commands 30/min, Wakes 3/min. Pricing: Data 500 requests per $1, Commands 1,000 per $1, Wakes 50 per $1, Streaming signals 150,000 per $1, with a $10 monthly discount. Every request with status <500 is billed. Polling vehicle_data at 1 Hz is about 3,600 requests/hour, roughly $7.20 per driving hour, and Tesla says regular polling 'is not recommended and will be expensive'.

Fleet Telemetry: the car streams over WebSocket and mTLS to a server you host. 'The event collector gathers data in 500 millisecond buckets', and a field is emitted only when interval_seconds has elapsed and its value has changed. Fields include VehicleSpeed (mph), PedalPosition (%), BrakePedal (bool), BrakePedalPos, Gear, DiAxleSpeedF/R (rad/s), DiTorqueActualF/R (Nm), LongitudinalAcceleration and LateralAcceleration. Tesla's docs give the acceleration unit as m/s^2; Teslemetry says Gs. Up to 5 third-party apps per vehicle.

Per-field minimum streaming intervals published by the Teslemetry relay: VehicleSpeed min 1 s, Gear min 1 s, BrakePedal min 1 s, Longitudinal/LateralAcceleration min 1 s, Location min 1 s. PedalPosition min 10 s, BrakePedalPos min 10 s, DiAxleSpeedF/R min 10 s, DiTorqueActualF/R min 10 s. Accelerator-pedal and motor data are therefore far too coarse for live engine sound.

Fleet API / Telemetry setup needs: a Tesla developer account with legal business details, an EC prime256v1 key pair with the public key at https://<domain>/.well-known/appspecific/com.tesla.3p.public-key.pem, partner registration in each region, a per-user OAuth third-party token (scopes vehicle_device_data and vehicle_location), the owner pairing the app's virtual key, and firmware 2023.20+ (2024.26+ via the command proxy; 2025.20+ for Intel Atom S/X; pre-2018 S/X not supported). Certificate setup has reportedly taken weeks.

The unofficial Owner API is deprecated: Tessie announced the end of a 90-day notice in mid-2024, and TeslaMate says it is being shut down for Business Fleet users and is still reachable for individuals for now. Its legacy streaming endpoint sent events about every second, but it is not a supported basis for a new product.

Real CAN-bus data (pedal, wipers, fan) can be read only with extra hardware, for example the Ctrl-Bridge on the OBD-II port. Ctrl-Bar itself uses Tesla's published BLE vehicle-command interface as an authorised virtual key. Neither path is available to a web page without a relay device.

Boombox / the external Pedestrian Warning System speaker works only in Park. Browser audio plays through the cabin media channel and the car's volume controls it. A web app cannot output to the exterior speaker while driving, so the 'exterior perspective' can only be a simulation inside the cabin.

Older Intel Atom (MCU2) cars run browser apps much more slowly than AMD Ryzen cars. In one app's own tests a 2019 Model 3 managed 10-15 fps on a general map engine. The DSP budget for the synth must be sized for Atom.

recommendations: Treat the touchscreen as the only guaranteed driver input. Use large on-screen UP/DOWN shift buttons; fire shift actions on pointerdown for low latency and set touch-action: manipulation. Lay out for devicePixelRatio 1.53 (and 1.0 on older firmware) using screen geometry, not UA, to detect the car.

Unlock audio only from an activation-triggering event: create or resume the AudioContext inside a click, pointerup or touchend handler, not a touch pointerdown, a gamepad press or a Media Session action. Show a 'Tap to start' or 'Tap to resume' overlay.

Watch AudioContext 'statechange' (suspended / interrupted) and the <audio> element's 'pause' event. When the car pauses browser audio (music change, call, scroll press), show a big resume button and call resume() from the next tap instead of looping on resume() from timers.

Make manual upshift via steering-wheel press an EXPERIMENTAL opt-in, not a core feature. Play the engine sound through an <audio> element whose srcObject comes from a MediaStreamAudioDestinationNode, so Chromium creates a media session. Set navigator.mediaSession.metadata and playbackState='playing'. Register setActionHandler for nexttrack (upshift), previoustrack (downshift), play and pause (keep audio running). Turn the feature on only after an in-car calibration step ('tilt the left scroll wheel right now') sees the event. Map shifting to tilt rather than press, because press means mute on Model Y and S/X and pause on Model 3 Highland.

Also add passive listeners for keydown/keyup (log key, code, keyCode), wheel and visibilitychange in a hidden diagnostics screen with an on-screen log and optional remote log upload, since the Tesla browser has no devtools. Use it to collect firmware/model-specific evidence before promising scroll-wheel shifting.

Offer optional Bluetooth gamepad shifting (e.g. a PS5 DualSense or a small paddle-style controller) through the Gamepad API. Poll navigator.getGamepads() at 30-60 Hz from requestAnimationFrame, guarded by a timing check because calls can stall more than 20 ms on Tesla. Map by standard-mapping position (with an A/B, X/Y swap toggle for 'TESLA VIRTUAL GAMEPAD' and Nintendo devices), and tell users to press a button once so the pad appears. It takes one of the car's two Bluetooth slots.
Don't build any input on Bluetooth keyboards, HID media remotes or keyboard events from the car; Tesla doesn't support them as page input.

Do NOT use the Fleet API or Fleet Telemetry for live load or RPM: pedal and motor data come every 10 s at best, speed every 1 s plus bucket and relay delay, it costs about $7/h if you poll vehicle_data, and it needs a backend, OAuth and a virtual key. Estimate load from GPS-derived acceleration plus the chosen Tesla model's mass and power, and run prediction and smoothing inside the AudioWorklet.

Generate all audio inside an AudioWorklet that keeps running on its own targets (RPM and load ramps, look-ahead extrapolation from 1 Hz GPS). Then 100-300 ms (up to multi-second) main-thread stalls and GPS gaps never cause glitches. Post parameter targets with timestamps rather than per-frame values, and keep a continuously running node so the context stays active.

Handle the browser being hidden in Reverse and full screen being blocked while moving: on visibilitychange hidden, ramp to idle or mute, and on visible resume smoothly. Don't rely on Fullscreen API while driving.
Serve from a real HTTPS domain (no raw IPs or LAN hosts; AudioWorklet needs a secure context), and test on an Intel Atom (MCU2) car to size the DSP budget.

Since the car raises media volume with speed ('Volume may be adjusted based on your driving speed'), don't add a separate speed-based loudness curve on top; keep loudness driven by RPM and load and let the user's volume wheel scale it.

verdicts.evidence: Fetched getrombo.com/faq: the question 'Can I shift gears with the steering-wheel buttons?' is answered 'Not for now. The car keeps those buttons for its own media player and doesn't pass them on to web pages, so Rombo shifts by itself, like an automatic.' verdicts.evidence: The README contains: 'Steering-wheel controls are not supported. The Tesla's scroll wheels/buttons have no path back to CarPlay through this setup.' The licence is BSD 3-Clause. verdicts.claim: A page playing an <audio> element gets a Tesla media widget showing page name/origin with generic previous/stop/next buttons (reporter photo, Sept 2026); nobody has confirmed whether those buttons or the wheel fire the page's Media Session handlers; PR lists Tesla as 'Not testable here'.
verdicts.evidence: Issue #135 (2026-09-15) says the widget reads 'Fuse Riders / andeplane.github.io with generic previous / stop / next buttons (Tesla screenshot from the reporter)'. PR #137 (merged 2026-09-15) says 'reporter's Tesla photo' and 'Not testable here: the real iPhone lock screen / Control Center and the Tesla widget'.
