verdicts.claim: Model Y manual: browser audio continues when minimised, Miniplayer can pause/play it, prior media resumes after browser audio pauses/ends, wheel tilt does next/prev, volume 'may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings'.
verdicts.evidence: The 2025-03-19 snapshot has the exact quotes: 'When you play audio through the web browser and then minimize the browser, Model Y continues the browser audio in the background. You can pause or play the browser audio through the media Miniplayer. If there was media playing before the browser audio began, the media resumes after you pause or end browser audio.' and 'Volume may be adjusted based on your driving speed and climate settings.' Caveat: the next/previous-by-scroll-button sentence sits in the internet radio/streaming-service paragraph, not the browser paragraph. The same page says pressing the left scroll button mutes.

verdicts.claim: Car pauses browser audio on music change/call, needs a tap; field log 2026-07-19 shows resume() refused until gesture; Tesla-specific fix keeps an inaudible oscillator running.
verdicts.evidence: Rombo FAQ: 'The sound stopped when I changed the music or took a call' → 'Tap to resume audio'. moonlight-web-stream-tsla stream.ts says: 'once the platform suspends the AudioContext, programmatic resume() is gated behind a user gesture (Tesla enforces this — 2026-07-19 field session: resume() was retried ~50x/s for the whole silent period and denied every time)'. stream/index.ts has keepAudioAlive, a 0.5 Hz oscillator at gain 0.00001 labelled 'Keep Audio Context Alive (Tesla Fix)'. Caveats: (1) keepAudioAlive defaults to TRUE, yet the code still needs a 'Tap to unmute' badge and 10-attempt warnings, so there is no evidence the oscillator stops platform suspension. (2) The states observed include 'interrupted', and in Chromium resume() on an interrupted context rejects with 'Cannot resume an interrupted AudioContext' whatever the gesture state. The 'needs a gesture' reading is the developer's inference.

verdicts.claim: Chrome Media Session routes hardware media keys to handlers; notification only for 'full' focus media ≥5 s; article only describes HTMLMediaElement so Web Audio-only output may not create a media session.
verdicts.evidence: The web.dev parts check out: 'full' audio focus, a minimum duration of at least 5 s, and hardware media keys supported. The Web Audio inference is wrong for current Chromium. Commit 2aeb1f458e (2025-01-06, 'MediaSession: Add WebAudio players as ambient players', crbug 382316461) registers AudioContexts with MediaSessionImpl as ambient players. MediaSessionImpl::IsControllable() returns true on non-Android when the routed service's playbackState != NONE. w3c/mediasession#378 (2026-09-24) says: 'Chromium: the AudioContext is producing audible output and playbackState is anything other than "none". Action handlers aren't required. The session is dropped after about 2 s of silence, or right away when the page calls suspend().' Whether Tesla's Miniplayer surfaces such an ambient-only session is untested.

verdicts.claim: Activation-triggering events are trusted keydown, mousedown, pointerdown(mouse), pointerup(touch/pen), touchend; touch pointerdown doesn't unlock audio; neither Gamepad input nor Media Session actions grant activation.
verdicts.evidence: The event list matches MDN. The Media Session part is wrong for Chromium. Blink MediaSession::DidReceiveAction calls LocalFrame::NotifyUserActivation(kInteraction): for every action up to commit 9030e52c0a (2026-09-08), and since then for every action except pause and stop. The commit message says 'Currently, user activation is granted when a page receives any media session action'. So a nexttrack/previoustrack/play action reaching the page grants user activation, and AudioContext.resume() inside that handler is allowed. Gamepad: correct that it is not in the spec. w3c/gamepad PR #230 'Trigger HTML activation' (2026-07-10) is still open. Also missed: MDN and Chromium gate Web Audio autoplay on STICKY activation (AutoplayPolicy::IsDocumentAllowedToPlay checks HasStickyUserActivation). After one qualifying tap, stock Chromium lets later programmatic resume() calls through, so the Tesla refusals are platform suspension or interruption, not a missing activation.

verdicts.claim: Keyboard/mouse don't work natively in Tesla browser; Tesla Bluetooth accepts only phones and game controllers, not HID keyboards; BT media remotes / keyboard paddles not viable.
verdicts.evidence: The moonlight-web-stream-tsla README says 'Tesla browser: keyboard and mouse do not work natively.' That is one third-party source and does not separate USB from Bluetooth. The manual reasoning is inaccurate. The Model 3 Bluetooth page also lists iPod Touch, iPad and Android tablets as pairable media devices, says 'up to twenty Bluetooth devices ... only allows two devices to connect simultaneously (such as one phone and one controller or two controllers)', and never mentions keyboards either way. The cited GUID-79A49D40 page is 'Theater, Arcade, and Toybox', not Bluetooth, and says 'Bluetooth Classic gaming controllers'. No source tested a Bluetooth media-remote (AVRCP/consumer-control) device. Such a device might reach the car's media layer, and so the Media Session path, rather than the page as keydown. Untested.

verdicts.claim: Browser works in Drive and plays audio while driving; no full screen while moving; browser disappears in Reverse; page can't change either.
verdicts.evidence: moonlight README: 'Works while parked, charging and in D mode'. Rombo FAQ: 'The Tesla browser doesn't allow full screen while the car is moving' and reverse is 'a limitation of the Tesla browser, and a web page can't change it'. Music-assistant discussion (2025-12-18): 'chromium-based web browser that can play audio during vehicle in drive'. The webspeak3 issue #8 independently shows the browser being minimised 'when the reverse camera opens'. All sources are third-party, with no Tesla doc. Note that 'disappears' means minimised, and minimising can stop non-media audio (see missed facts).

verdicts.claim: AudioWorklet works in Tesla browser over HTTPS; main thread stalls 100-300 ms on cellular micro-outages and seconds (3.3-16.3 s) during modem recovery; no devtools.
verdicts.evidence: AudioWorklet working: supported. The EV·ENGINE public stats API reports platform 'Tesla': 151 audio starts and 0 AudioWorklet fallbacks. Its browser-support page lists the Tesla browser as 'Full support' for AudioWorklet, and moonlight comments describe on-device worklet behaviour. No devtools: supported (freeze_watch.ts: 'without devtools, which the Tesla browser doesn't have'). The stall part is misread from the source. freeze_watch.ts describes the 100-300 ms events as the cellular downlink pausing ('the pipe just stops for 100-300ms and then bursts. Confirmed on Tesla 2026-07-15: rx spiked ... with 0 loss and a healthy rAF'). That is a network stall with a HEALTHY main thread. Only the radio-outage/modem-recovery events (3.3/4.5/16.3 s rAF gaps) and one 3.9 s 'main-thread-stall' were main-thread freezes. These numbers come from a heavy WebRTC streaming app and may not carry over to an offline GPS page. The advice to generate audio on the audio thread still stands.

corrections: Media Session actions DO grant user activation in Chromium (Blink MediaSession::DidReceiveAction → LocalFrame::NotifyUserActivation). This held for all actions until 2026-09-08 and for all except pause/stop since commit 9030e52c0a. If a wheel tilt reaches the page as nexttrack/previoustrack, the handler may legitimately call AudioContext.resume(). Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/modules/mediasession/media_session.cc

Chromium Web Audio autoplay is gated on STICKY activation (AutoplayPolicy::IsDocumentAllowedToPlay → HasStickyUserActivation), not on a fresh gesture. Repeated resume() refusals on Tesla therefore point to platform suspension or the AudioContext 'interrupted' state ('Cannot resume an interrupted AudioContext'), not missing activation. Pages should handle the 'interrupted' state in onstatechange. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/modules/webaudio/audio_context.cc

Web Audio-only output CAN create a controllable media session in Chromium. Since Jan 2025, AudioContexts register as 'ambient' MediaSession players (commit 2aeb1f458e), and the session becomes controllable on non-Android when navigator.mediaSession.playbackState != 'none'. It is dropped after ~2 s of silence or on suspend(). Tesbox should set playbackState='playing' plus metadata and handlers. Sources: https://github.com/w3c/mediasession/issues/378 and https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/commits/2aeb1f458e

The 100-300 ms Tesla 'stalls' in moonlight freeze_watch.ts are cellular downlink pauses with a healthy rAF/main thread. Only modem-recovery outages (3.3/4.5/16.3 s) and one 3.9 s event were main-thread freezes.

Claim 11 cites GUID-79A49D40, which is the 'Theater, Arcade, and Toybox' page, not Bluetooth. The real Bluetooth page (GUID-3D90EA76) also allows tablets and iPods as media devices and is silent on keyboards. 'Only phones and game controllers' is an overstatement.

'Every documented scroll-wheel function is car-level' is inaccurate. The manual documents wheel buttons driving native apps: Arcade games ('You may need to use the steering wheel buttons') and Toybox Emissions ('press the left scroll wheel'). The routing exists for native apps; there is just no documented browser path.

The moonlight 'Keep Audio Context Alive (Tesla Fix)' oscillator defaults to ON (settings_menu.ts), yet the same code still ships a 'Tap to unmute' recovery badge for the 2026-07-19 failure. There is no evidence the inaudible oscillator prevents platform suspension. At gain 1e-5 it is also likely below Chromium's audibility threshold, so it would not keep a Web Audio media session alive.

Model Y Media page (Mar 2025): pressing the left scroll button MUTES all volume, and in a call it mutes sound and mic. On such cars, a 'press to upshift' gesture would also mute Tesbox. On the 2026 Model 3, press = play/pause media. If Tesbox is the active media source, that would likely send a pause action, which since Sept 2026 Chromium no longer grants activation for.
missed: Tesla minimise/background risk for Web Audio: webspeak3 issue #8 (Model Y, 2026-09-11). Minimising the browser (reverse camera, switching to the nav map) stopped Web Audio/WebRTC output, and 'the vehicle's OS assumes the browser is no longer playing media and immediately starts playing the car radio'. Discord web survived. A maintainer's source analysis (untested in car) says Tesla keeps browser audio only for pages that appear in the Miniplayer, i.e. a controllable Chromium media session. The proposed workaround is a >5 s near-silent (~-61 dBFS) looping <audio> file element plus mediaSession metadata, playbackState and play/pause handlers. Chromium's DurationToMediaContentType makes media of 5 s or less 'transient' (not controllable). https://github.com/Moepchi/webspeak3/issues/8 and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/media/base/media_content_type.cc

A route to test wheel shifting: if Tesbox becomes the active media session (audible Web Audio with playbackState='playing', or a >5 s <audio> element), Tesla's Miniplayer prev/next and possibly the wheel tilt may arrive as nexttrack/previoustrack. In Chromium these also grant user activation. Map tilt-right = upshift and tilt-left = downshift rather than relying on press, since press is mute or pause. Nobody has tested this; it needs an in-car test harness that logs Media Session actions and keydown (MediaTrackNext/MediaTrackPrevious).

FrontierCloud (2026-09-28) observed Tesla Chromium backgrounded-playback failures after an OTA. The renderer stopped progressing in the gap between one media element ending and the next starting, and the fix was a warm standby element started 200 ms before the end. It also dedupes duplicate 'MediaSession next/previous' and 'MediaTrackNext/MediaTrackPrevious' system signals within 900 ms ('Some embedded systems can emit more than one system media-control signal for one physical transition'). This suggests Tesla-originated next/prev can reach pages, possibly twice. Low confidence: Tesla is not named for that specific behaviour. https://github.com/wongyiuming/FrontierCloud/pull/56

Tesla browser GPS caveats: first fixes arrived up to 91 s old even with watchPosition maximumAge: 2000, so the Tesla browser appears to ignore maximumAge and position.timestamp must be checked (frunky field traces). Car-browser GPS is ~1 Hz with ~1 s lag (frunky README; EV·ENGINE /tesla: 'GPS reports a fix about once a second'). https://github.com/clemenshelm/frunky/issues/9 and https://ev-engine.com/tesla

The Tesla browser caches HTML indefinitely: frunky's car 'drove a build five deploys old'. Serve HTML with Cache-Control: no-store or a versioned service-worker update flow. Relevant to the offline PWA. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/clemenshelm/frunky/HEAD/README.md

The Tesla browser blocks local/private IP access; you need a real domain, with HTTPS recommended. AudioWorklet and geolocation need a secure context anyway, so in-car dev testing needs a public HTTPS host. https://github.com/Waliers/moonlight-web-stream-tsla

Tesla Gamepad specifics: controllers can appear as 'TESLA VIRTUAL GAMEPAD' (also vendor 045e/045a, product 02d1). The virtual pad maps Nintendo controllers by label rather than position, so A/B and X/Y need swapping. The manual supports only 'Bluetooth Classic' controllers, with at most two connected Bluetooth devices per screen (phone plus controller). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Waliers/moonlight-web-stream-tsla/HEAD/moonlight-web/web-server/web/stream/gamepad.ts

Measured Tesla Web Audio output latency from EV·ENGINE's public aggregate stats: Tesla avg ~98.6 ms, max 435 ms (n=151), with 0 AudioWorklet fallbacks. The page plays through the car's media channel, so the car's media volume governs it. https://ev-engine.com/api/stats and https://ev-engine.com/tesla

Model 3 2026: pressing both wheels briefly opens the secondary P/R/N/D selector. A two-thumb shift gesture must never be suggested, and a left-wheel press gesture risks accidental chords while driving. https://web.archive.org/web/20260313071914/https://www.tesla.com/ownersmanual/model3/en_us/GUID-DEB259CC-ABAC-4BFC-8D10-B7B1BBCFCB1F.html

research.summary: Clean room: nothing was opened from rupteur.app. Every search excluded that domain. The research supports a physically informed design: a pulse train driven by the firing order, fed into digital waveguides, written as a single AudioWorklet (WASM preferred). Industry Active Sound Design (ASD) uses order synthesis, which means sine waves at multiples of RPM. Its own vendors say pure order synthesis sounds "rigid and idealized" and needs cycle-to-cycle variation to sound natural (Bodden & Belschner, Inter-noise 2014). Physically informed models get firing-order character (cross-plane V8 burble, the inline-5 off-beat, unequal-length boxer rumble) directly from crank-angle timing and per-cylinder delays. The best-documented recipe is Baldan et al. 2015 (cylinders, intake, extractor, muffler and outlet as interconnected waveguides, controlled by RPM and throttle). The 2026 PTR paper (Doerfler & Wyse) shows exhaust-pulse trains fed into Karplus-Strong resonators reconstruct harmonics 21% better than harmonic-plus-noise. It also gives gating functions for throttle and fuel-cut (DFCO) states. Open-source references with usable licences: Antonio-R1 engine-sound-generator (MIT, Web Audio, AudioWorklet+WASM, implements Baldan), DasEtwas/enginesound (MIT, Rust), ange-yaghi/engine-sim (MIT, 10 kHz physical sim plus convolution impulse responses (IRs), Windows-only, now moved to a community edition), EngineLab (MIT, C++/JUCE; V8/V12 can miss real time on modest CPUs). Not usable in a commercial product: SDT (GPLv3, copyleft), PTR code and the 2026 dataset (CC BY-NC/NC-SA), Farnell's Pd patches (no licence stated). Granular or sample approaches add risks: recording licences (BOOM's EULA bars sample-playback systems), offline asset size, and live Harman patents on PSOLA (pitch-synchronous overlap-add) resynthesis and harmonic+residual analysis of engine recordings (US 12,243,510, expires ~2043; US 9,553,553, expires 2035). The DSP fits a weak CPU easily (an estimated ~400 ops/sample, well under 5% of one core). The real risks are GC and allocation in process(), main-thread contention, and the fixed 128-frame quantum (2.67 ms at 48 kHz). Tesla's browser is on Chromium 140 (2026.14) and reportedly 148 (2026.26), so AudioWorklet should work, but renderSizeHint (Chrome 153) is not available yet.

claims.claim: Baldan, Lachambre, Delle Monache & Boussard (IEEE SIVE 2015) describe a procedural, physically informed engine model. Cylinders, intakes, extractors, straight pipe, muffler and outlet are each mutually interacting digital waveguides. Each cylinder waveguide is excited by piston motion p(x)=cos(4πx) and a fuel-ignition half-sine of width t. Valve functions (exhaust: -sin(4πx) for 0.75<x<1; intake: sin(4πx) for 0<x<0.25) modulate the valve-end reflection. The phasor frequency is f=RPM/120.

In the Baldan model, intake waveguides have fixed free-end feedback -0.5 and extractors 0.1. Intakes also get lowpass-filtered white noise, amplitude-modulated by the intake-valve function (turbulence). Ignition amplitude is modulated by throttle. 'Cycle asymmetry' shifts cylinder phases to create low-RPM oscillation and high-RPM 'growl'.

The Baldan model has three listening outputs: intake (under hood), engine-block vibration (lowpass of piston motion plus ignitions, 'mainly heard in the cabin') and outlet (rear of vehicle). The muffler is 4 parallel, partially reflecting waveguides with lengths chosen so each frequency peaks in at most one element. Its 'action' parameter runs from 0 (very loud) to 1 (silent).

Baldan models backfire (overrun pops) as a Poisson-like process. While RPM is falling, each cycle compares a probability against a random value. On a hit, an ignition-like impulse goes into the exhaust outlet and the probability is squared, so it decays exponentially.

Baldan reports low computational cost and no audible delay in informal tests. The authors say modal synthesis and comb filters did not give the desired quality compared with waveguides. Their sample-vs-synthetic spectrogram comparison showed the synthetic version had less mid-high energy (it was darker).

Farnell's Designing Sound engine model assumes the main acoustic contribution is exhaust gas expelled through the exhaust valves, not combustion inside the sealed chamber. Each cylinder adds a positive half-cosine pulse every two cycles into a 4-quadrant feedback delay chain, plus FM and waveshaping. Baldan et al. judge that it lacks higher harmonics and is hard to control.

Farnell's Practical 22 (Cars) Pure Data files (toy_boat_engine.pd, pulse_demo.pd parabolic pulses, jitter_engine.pd, waveguide_engine.pd 'warped waveguide') are published on aspress.co.uk with no licence stated. Treat them as all-rights-reserved and use only the ideas.

Antonio-R1/engine-sound-generator is MIT-licensed JavaScript/Web Audio code based on Baldan et al. 2015. Its first version (AudioBufferSourceNode.start scheduling) misbehaved in some browsers. The second uses an AudioWorklet. A C++/Emscripten WASM port of the worklet was made 'more efficient' and removed the glitches of the JS version.

DasEtwas/enginesound is MIT-licensed Rust, loosely based on Baldan et al. It does pseudo-realistic pipe and chamber simulation (speed of sound, pipe-end reflection), mixes intake, exhaust and engine vibration, includes resonance damping, and defaults to 48 kHz.

ange-yaghi/engine-sim (AngeTheGreat) is MIT-licensed. It simulates at 10 kHz by default and writes delayed per-cylinder exhaust flow to a synthesizer for each exhaust system. The delay is (header primary + exhaust length)/343 m/s, scaled by 1/length². The synthesizer adds jitter/noise, a DC block, convolution with an IR (capped at 10,000 samples), lowpass filtering and a leveler. The repo builds only on Windows, the author calls the code 'sloppy', and the project has moved to a community edition that is no longer actively maintained.

engine-sim ships an impulse-response sound library (es/sound-library with archive/new/sharp/smooth folders) inside the MIT-licensed repo. It could be reused, with attribution, as convolution colouring for an 'exterior' perspective.

EngineLab (zolaski333, MIT, C++20/JUCE) derives exhaust sound from simulated cylinder pressure through a quasi-1D duct and waveguide network. Its README says large engines (V8, V12) may fall below real time on modest CPUs. Full gas-dynamic simulation is therefore too heavy for a Tesla MCU2 browser.

The Sound Design Toolkit (SDT), which includes a combustion-engine model from the Baldan/Delle Monache group, is GPLv3-or-later. Its code cannot go into a closed or permissively licensed Tesbox without copyleft obligations.

The PTR model (Doerfler & Wyse, arXiv 2603.09391, 2026) treats engine sound as sequential exhaust pressure pulses. Each pulse is an asymmetric envelope E=(1-exp(-αφ))exp(-βφ) multiplied by a decaying harmonic sum (a_k ∝ e^(-0.5kλ)), with phase bending φ̃=2π(φ/2π)^ν for the thermodynamic pitch drop. The pulses feed Karplus-Strong resonators: two per bank plus one shared resonator for the common pipe. The V8 firing order is [1,5,4,8,6,3,7,2], with per-cylinder timing offsets of up to ±40°.

PTR gates noise by operating regime: throttle factor g_thr=max(torque,ε)^0.7 (ε=0.02) and DFCO factor max(-torque,ε). Turbulence is amplitude modulation of pulses times g_thr, and there is a separate airflow noise during fuel cut. PTR beat a harmonic-plus-noise baseline by 21% on harmonic reconstruction (5.7% total loss), trained at 16 kHz.

The PTR code and weights are CC BY-NC 4.0, and the Procedural Engine Sounds dataset is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Neither the code nor the data can be used commercially. Only the published ideas can be reimplemented independently.

Doerfler & Wyse's dataset synthesizer is harmonic-plus-noise with 128 sine oscillators. It covers orders 0.5 to 64 in 0.5 steps, with RPM/torque-dependent inharmonicity, pink-noise amplitude modulation for combustion turbulence, and filtered noise modulated by orders 0.5-2 for valve and mechanical events. Exhaust resonances use parallel feedback delays.

Order-based synthesis (sine waves at engine orders set by RPM and firing order, with gain from load and pedal) is the standard automotive Active Sound Design method. Neosonic's authors, who build ASD systems, say it is 'rigid and idealized' and neglects cylinder-to-cylinder and cycle-to-cycle micro-variation, which must be added for natural sound. Heavy character changes (e.g., I4 made to sound like a V8) tend to sound artificial.

In perception studies of driving sound, pleasantness explained 58% of variance and powerfulness/sportiness 23%. Synthetic sound should therefore be tuned for pleasantness over long exposure, not just aggression.

Michon et al.'s Stanford driving simulator (SMC 2016) synthesised engine sound in Faust from an aperiodic pulse-train generator fed through filters. To reproduce the closed-window car shell they applied 4th-order lowpass filters at 500 Hz to cabin speakers, and 90 Hz for the seat shaker. The whole engine of 28 sources plus reverb used 12% of a Mac Mini CPU.

Alkmim, Colangeli, Bodden et al. (Forum Acusticum 2023) convolve synthesized ASD sound with measured cabin IRs (loudspeaker to driver) to add the propagation path for off-vehicle evaluation. Tesbox plays through real cabin speakers, so the real cabin already supplies its own IR. Tesbox's 'cabin perspective' should model the engine-to-cabin transmission path, not add cabin reverb.

A crossplane V8 fires every 90° overall (LRLLRLRR-type bank sequence), but each bank sees uneven intervals of 180-90-180-270°. When each bank's 4 ports merge into one exit, this gives the characteristic burble. Racing '180° headers' even it out. The crossplane inline-4 (Yamaha R1) fires at 90-180-270-180.

Typical firing orders: inline-4 1-3-4-2 (some British 1-2-4-3), inline-5 1-2-4-5-3 (144° spacing), inline-6 1-5-3-6-2-4. V6 60°: R1-L1-R2-L2-R3-L3 (120° even). V6 90° odd-fire alternates 90°/150°; split-pin versions get even 120°. Flat-6 is 120°. 90° V-twin is 270°/450°. Uneven intervals give a 'burble/throaty/growling' sound; even ones sound smoother.

The Subaru boxer rumble comes from unequal-length exhaust headers, not the boxer layout. Pulses reach the collector at uneven times, giving a pattern of a strong (merged) pulse followed by a weaker one. In a synth this is reproduced by giving each cylinder its own header delay before the collector.

The main exhaust noise source is the blowdown pressure pulse when the exhaust valve opens while cylinder pressure is still high. Intake and exhaust noise sits at the firing frequency and its multiples. Flow and turbulence noise is a secondary broadband source above about 400 Hz.

The speed of sound in an exhaust system varies with temperature from about 319 m/s (-20 °C) to 841 m/s (850 °C). Pipe resonances such as quarter-wave f=c/(4L) therefore shift with exhaust temperature. A cold-start-to-warm drift of resonances is physically justified.

Expansion-chamber muffler transmission loss is TL=10·log10[1+¼(m−1/m)²·sin²(kL)], where m is the area ratio and k=2πf/c. It peaks at kL=odd·π/2 and is zero at kL=nπ. The Helmholtz resonator frequency is f=(c/2π)·sqrt(A/(V·L_eq)), and Helmholtz chambers are used in intakes (Viper V10) and exhausts to shape the note.

Factory valved sports exhausts (e.g., Porsche PSE) have two gas paths and a flap. Closed means through the mufflers; open means a straighter path bypassing them, which is louder with more burble and crackle. The flap is controlled by mode button and ECU mapping, and on some models reopens around 3,300 RPM with moderate throttle.

Game audio practice (Mike Caviezel, BOOM primer) for off-throttle: remove the intake layer, drop the engine layer a few dB, and EQ out about 2 kHz midrange and about 10 kHz treble from the exhaust. On full throttle, optionally add distortion and low-end boost. Loops are typically every 500 RPM (250 RPM at low revs), because pitch-shifting beyond about ±500 RPM sounds stretched.

Turbocharger tones sit at integer orders of shaft speed. The synchronous (1st-order, unbalance) whistle is at shaft rev/s. Blade-pass frequency is blades × rev/s and can reach about 30 kHz, so it is often inaudible. Shaft speeds of about 80-150 krpm are cited. Broadband compressor 'whoosh' near surge is about 4-12 kHz for spark-ignition engines (1.5-3 kHz for diesel).

Turbo flutter is compressor surge when the throttle closes under boost and there is no blow-off valve (BOV): air separates from the blades, reverses, the pressure drops, the blades re-grip, and the cycle repeats as a 'choofing' flutter. The noise comes from the turbo itself. Surge oscillation is low-frequency, about 1-20 Hz, set by the Helmholtz resonance of the compressor ducts.

'Pops and bangs' on overrun come from partially suppressing deceleration fuel cut and heavily retarding ignition, so combustion finishes in the exhaust manifold. They need a rich mixture, retarded timing and a free-flowing exhaust.

Rev limiters cut spark or fuel. Ignition cut is instant and can hold near-constant RPM. Fuel cut is more violent, with bigger RPM swings and lean cycles. A 'soft' cut drops fewer or shorter events and RPM holds. A 'hard' cut drops RPM noticeably and bounces.
In a four-stroke engine the camshaft turns at half crank speed. Valve events therefore repeat once per 720°, at RPM/120 per valve, which sets the period for valvetrain tick synthesis.

Granular and analysis/resynthesis engine audio needs real recordings. Crankcase REV slices accel/decel 'ramp' recordings at individual piston firings. UE MotoSynth and GTA V-style granular systems need ramp recordings per vehicle. Loop-based systems need about 13 loops per perspective (about 52 files for 4 perspectives) for one car.

Commercial SFX licences such as BOOM Library's forbid stand-alone redistribution, use 'in the clear', and embedding 'for the purpose of ... any form of musical sample or sound effect sample playback system'. An engine-sound playback app built from purchased recordings is high risk under such terms.
Freesound content is CC0, CC-BY or CC-BY-NC. Only CC0 and CC-BY can be used commercially, and CC-BY needs attribution.

US copyright protects sound recordings (17 USC 102(a)(7)) but not ideas, procedures, processes, systems or methods (102(b)). Algorithms from published papers and engine facts (firing orders, dimensions) can be reimplemented. Recordings and code cannot be copied without a licence.

Harley-Davidson's 1994 attempt to register its V-twin exhaust sound as a trademark drew opposition from nine manufacturers and was withdrawn in 2000. Engine sounds are hard to monopolise, but brand-named engine presets still carry trademark and passing-off questions.

Live patents cover sample-based engine synthesis. Harman US 12,243,510 B2 (granted Mar 4 2025, filed Oct 2022) covers pitch-modified engine sound made by selecting segments of recorded samples with synchronous pitch overlap-add. Harman US 9,553,553 B2 (expires 2035) covers harmonic+residual analysis/resynthesis of input engine noise. Hyundai/Kia US 11,904,769 B2 (expires 2042) covers user-customised virtual engine sound updated by an emotion model and reviews.

US 6,959,094 B1 (Staccato-era physical-model synthesis of internal-combustion engine vehicle sounds; Cascone, Scandalis, Stilson, Van Duyne et al.) was filed Apr 16 2001 and granted Nov 2005, so it has expired. The general idea of physically modelled engine sound is old prior art.

AudioWorklet shipped by default in Chrome 66. It runs user code on the audio rendering thread, unlike the deprecated ScriptProcessorNode, which runs on the main thread. The render quantum is 128 frames, so the budget is about 3 ms at 44.1 kHz (2.67 ms at 48 kHz). A GC pause or slow process() causes glitches. Chrome recommends WASM to avoid JIT/GC overhead and pre-allocating everything.

In AudioWorklet process(), an a-rate parameter array has 128 values, or a single value if not automated. A k-rate array always has 1 value. Code must check array lengths and always return true for a source node. An uncaught exception silences the node permanently.

The configurable render quantum (AudioContext renderSizeHint) shipped only in Chrome 153, after an origin trial from Chrome 145. Tesla's browser is on Chromium 140 (update 2026.14, up from 136) and reportedly 148 (2026.26). Tesbox must assume 128-frame quanta.

Tesla infotainment: MCU2 uses an Intel Atom (low-power, described as roughly 2x slower than MCU3; Netflix launch about 20 s vs 4 s). MCU3 uses an AMD Ryzen (Zen+ quad-core) and has been standard on all new Teslas since about 2025. Some newer browser features are restricted to Ryzen cars.

Native Web Audio node costs: BiquadFilter is cheap (about 5 multiplies and 4 adds per sample). ConvolverNode is 'very expensive' and grows with IR length (FFT, partly on a background thread). WaveShaper is cheap without oversampling. OscillatorNode uses band-limited inverse-FFT wavetables. Linux/PulseAudio output latency is typically 30-40 ms, and higher latency hints allow bigger, more efficient rendering.

AudioContext accepts latencyHint 'interactive' (default, lowest glitch-free latency), 'balanced', 'playback' (lowest power), or a number of seconds. It also accepts a sampleRate option (typically 8-96 kHz); otherwise the output device's preferred rate is used.

Emscripten Wasm Audio Worklets (-sAUDIO_WORKLET -sWASM_WORKERS) run C/C++ callbacks on the real-time audio thread with 'no temporary JavaScript level VM garbage'. The default mode needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs COOP/COEP cross-origin isolation. A 'worklet' environment with SINGLE_FILE avoids SharedArrayBuffer.
Faust can compile DSP to WebAssembly AudioWorklet nodes via faustwasm. The licence terms for generated code and the Faust standard libraries were not confirmed in this research.

Other browser procedural engine projects exist. YigitSalihEmecen/Engine_Sim (MIT) renders each bank's 720° cycle of combustion pulses at the firing angles, differentiates it, and FFTs it into PeriodicWave tables for native OscillatorNodes, plus waveguide exhaust, collector and reactive muffler. TheFantazer/engine_sound (AudioWorklet pulse-train plus pipe resonators plus Helmholtz intake; licence unverified). VinZu17/Engine-Sound-Simulator (MIT, oscillator plus sample hybrid). cemrich/js-motor-sound-generation (MIT).

Chrome Racer (2013) dropped multi-RPM sample layers for 3 files (accel with gears, decel, idle) because many loops cost too much to download and wide pitch-shifting sounded synthetic. Generated audio was avoided there to save CPU for visuals on weak devices.

The missing-fundamental effect lets speakers that cannot reproduce low frequencies suggest them by playing the harmonics (e.g., MaxxBass). This can serve virtual bass for low firing frequencies, such as an I4 idling at 800 RPM (about 26.7 Hz), on Teslas without a subwoofer.

The Hyundai Ioniq 5 N ships the production equivalent of Tesbox's concept. N e-Shift simulates an 8-speed DCT through motor-torque interruption and rev-matched downshifts. N Active Sound+ plays selectable virtual sounds ('Ignition' = turbo N petrol engine, 'Evolution', 'Supersonic') through 10 speakers.

recommendations: Core method: build the firing-order pulse train plus digital waveguides, following Baldan 2015 and refined with PTR-style pulse shapes and regime gating, written from the papers in Tesbox's own code. Do not use order-only additive synthesis or granular samples as the core. This gives crossplane, inline-5, odd-fire V6 and unequal-length boxer character directly from data. It avoids recording licences, offline asset size and the Harman PSOLA and harmonic+residual patents.

Use one AudioWorkletNode called 'engine-core', written in C/C++ or Rust compiled to WASM (Emscripten Wasm Audio Worklets in 'worklet'/SINGLE_FILE mode, so no SharedArrayBuffer or COOP/COEP is needed), with a pure-JS fallback of the same algorithm. Pre-allocate all buffers. Do no allocation, closures or postMessage handling in the hot path. Always return true. Handle param arrays of length 1 or 128. Assume 128-frame quanta, because renderSizeHint is unavailable before Chromium 153.

Control-plane split: the main thread runs at 30-60 Hz. It interpolates GPS speed (about 1 Hz) to a smooth speed, converts it to RPM through the gearbox model, and estimates load in [-1, 1] (negative = overrun/DFCO) from acceleration and the selected Tesla's mass and power. Continuous values go to the worklet as k-rate AudioParams (rpm, load, exhaustValve, perspective mix, volume) and are re-smoothed inside the worklet with one-pole filters (about 30-80 ms). Rare events (shift, limiter mode, preset change) go over MessagePort.

Engine preset is pure data (JSON), not audio. It holds cylinder count, per-cylinder firing angle (0-720°), bank id, header primary length per cylinder (m), collector topology, mid-pipe, 3-4 muffler chamber lengths, tailpipe length, intake runner length, airbox Helmholtz frequency, idle and redline RPM, limiter type (soft/hard, fuel/ignition), turbo (max shaft krpm, spool time constant, BOV vs flutter) and crackle propensity. Firing orders and dimensions are facts and methods (17 USC 102(b)); describe presets generically to avoid trademark issues.

Pulse generator: keep a double-precision crank-phase accumulator over 720°. At each cylinder's firing angle, plus small random per-cycle jitter (about ±1°) and amplitude variation (about ±5%), emit a smooth asymmetric blowdown pulse E=(1−e^(−αφ))e^(−βφ) about 40-90 crank degrees wide. Amplitude is 0.15 + 0.85·g_thr, with g_thr = max(load, 0.02)^0.7. Brightness, via pulse sharpness or a one-pole tilt, rises with load. Smooth pulses keep aliasing low at 48 kHz. Add 'cycle asymmetry' as a per-preset growl control (Baldan).

Exhaust path: give each cylinder a header delay of L_i/c_hot (c about 450-600 m/s, warming from about 350 m/s at cold start). Sum per bank into a collector waveguide. Then a mid-pipe waveguide, 3-4 parallel partially reflecting muffler waveguides, and a tailpipe/outlet waveguide, each with a one-pole lowpass loss in the loop. Unequal header lengths and per-bank collectors reproduce the boxer rumble and crossplane burble with no special-casing.

Exhaust valve: closed means a high muffler 'action' (more reflection and cancellation) plus extra lowpass (cut about 2 kHz and 10 kHz). Open means a bypass straight path with low action and more highs and level. Crossfade over about 150-300 ms. Auto mode opens above a mode-dependent RPM/load threshold (factory systems reopen around 3,300 rpm with throttle) and raises crackle probability when open.

Intake and induction: lowpass noise gated by each cylinder's intake-valve window, scaled by g_thr (silent off-throttle), through a bandpass at the airbox Helmholtz frequency. Mechanical layer: engine-block vibration (lowpass of piston motion plus ignition, Baldan) and a quiet valvetrain tick of filtered noise bursts on valve events (RPM/120 per valve).

Turbo: keep a shaft-speed state that lags the target (load × RPM) with a time constant of about 0.3-1.5 s. Produce a whistle as 1-2 sines at the 1st order of shaft speed (1-4 kHz audible range) plus a noise 'whoosh' band (4-12 kHz) scaled by boost². On throttle lift with boost above a threshold, either play a BOV noise burst (bandpassed, fast attack, about 0.3-0.8 s decay) or flutter (whoosh amplitude-modulated at 8-20 Hz, decaying, from surge physics).

Overrun and limiter: when load < 0 and RPM is falling, run a Poisson pop process (rate set by preset × valve-open factor, decaying exponentially per Baldan). Inject impulsive bursts into the collector or outlet waveguide so they ring through the exhaust resonances, and add DFCO airflow noise scaled by max(−load, ε). Rev limiter: skip combustion pulses (all cylinders for a hard cut, a subset for a soft cut) with RPM hysteresis. Ignition-cut mode adds pop events, fuel-cut mode does not.

Perspectives: exterior is mainly the outlet plus some intake, full bandwidth, with an optional short MIT IR from engine-sim's sound library. Cabin is a transmission-path model: a 4th-order lowpass around 400-800 Hz on airborne exhaust and intake (Michon used 500 Hz), more weight on the engine-block layer below about 250 Hz, and the turbo whistle kept faintly audible. Do not add cabin reverb, because the real cabin supplies it.

Output stage: DC blocker, then per-Tesla-model bass management. Without a subwoofer, high-pass about 50-80 Hz and add a virtual-bass harmonic generator (missing fundamental) for firing frequencies below the corner. With a subwoofer, high-pass about 25-30 Hz. Finish with a soft limiter and safety clipper, because resonant waveguides can blow up.

Context settings: start the AudioContext from a user gesture. Use latencyHint 'balanced' (fall back to 'playback' on MCU2, since GPS-driven RPM changes don't need low latency) and the device sample rate. Expose a 'Lite' quality tier for MCU2: fewer muffler sections, shared header delays per bank, no IR convolution, fewer noise bands.

Test on real cars before committing. Run an on-car CPU stress page on MCU2 (Atom) and MCU3 (Ryzen) that measures process() time per quantum and counts glitches with the map and other tabs active. Ship WASM and JS builds and pick at runtime based on measured headroom.

Keep the clean-room record. Log the source of every algorithm (Baldan 2015, Farnell 2010, PTR 2026, Wikipedia firing orders). Copy no code from GPL, NC or unlicensed repos. Code from MIT repos may be adapted with attribution kept in a NOTICES file.

Have a patent professional run a freedom-to-operate check on EV virtual-engine-sound patents (Harman, Hyundai/Kia and others) before launch, especially for gear-shift simulation and user customisation features.

verdicts.claim: Baldan, Lachambre, Delle Monache & Boussard (IEEE SIVE 2015): procedural physically informed model; cylinders, intakes, extractors, straight pipe, muffler, outlet are mutually interacting digital waveguides; cylinder excited by piston p(x)=cos(4πx) and ignition half-sine of width t; exhaust valve -sin(4πx) on 0.75<x<1, intake sin(4πx) on 0<x<0.25 modulate valve-end reflection; phasor f=RPM/120.
verdicts.evidence: Full text read (DOI 10.1109/SIVE.2015.7361287). Sec 3.3: components 'treated as resonant cavities and represented by mutually interacting digital waveguides'. Sec 3.1 gives e(x)=-sin(4πx) for 0.75<x<1, i(x)=sin(4πx) for 0<x<0.25, p(x)=cos(4πx), and f=RPM/120 with one phasor ramp per two crank revolutions. Valves 'modulate the feedback coefficients' (open sends the signal to the output, closed recirculates it). Caveat: the printed ignition formula s(x)=sin(2π(xt+0.5)) on 0<x<t contradicts the text. It gives a negative lobe and puts ignition at the start of the cycle, overlapping the intake window, whereas the text says 'positive half of a sine wave, shifted at the beginning of the expansion phase'. 'Width t' is the intended meaning (t: 0 = instantaneous, 1 = full cycle). The piston motion also modulates the cylinder waveguide's delay time, which the claim omits.

verdicts.claim: Baldan: intake free-end feedback -0.5, extractors 0.1; intakes get lowpass white noise AM'd by intake valve; ignition amplitude modulated by throttle; cycle asymmetry gives low-RPM oscillation and high-RPM growl.
verdicts.evidence: Verbatim: 'fixed feedback on the free end (-0.5 for intakes, 0.1 for extractors) and variable feedback on the valve end'. 'Intakes are fed with ... lowpass-filtered white noise, modulated in amplitude by the intake valve function'. 'Ignitions are modulated in amplitude by the throttle load'. Asymmetric phase shifting 'results in a sound with an oscillatory character at low regimes and a growling voice at higher rates'. The cycle-asymmetry parameter runs from 0 (symmetric) to 1 (cylinders overlap).

verdicts.claim: Baldan: three outputs (intake/under hood, engine-block = lowpass of piston+ignitions 'mainly heard in the cabin', outlet/rear); muffler = 4 parallel partially reflecting waveguides with lengths so each frequency peaks in at most one; action 0 very loud to 1 silent.
verdicts.evidence: Verbatim: 'four independent, partially reflecting waveguides'. 'Delay lines are set so that every frequency has a peak in the frequency response of at most one element'. The muffler elements are 'connected in parallel to the outlet'. Muffler action runs from '0 being very loud' to '1 being completely silent'. The outputs are: summed intake free ends (listening point 'under the hood'), lowpass of piston motions plus ignitions ('mainly heard in the cabin'), and outlet free end ('rear of the vehicle').

verdicts.claim: Baldan backfire: Poisson-like; while RPM falling, each cycle compares probability vs random; on hit, ignition-like impulse into exhaust outlet and probability squared, so decays exponentially.
verdicts.evidence: Verbatim: 'Backfiring is modeled as a Poisson process. When ... RPM are decreasing, at every full cycle a probability factor is tested against a random value ... an impulsive signal, similar to the fuel ignition function ... is added to the input of the exhaust outlet. At every backfire the probability factor is multiplied by itself, yielding an exponential decrease.' Nuances: squaring gives p^(2^n) after n backfires, which is doubly exponential in the backfire count. The paper gives no rule for resetting the probability. The authors' conclusions single out the backfiring algorithm as needing improvement.

verdicts.claim: Farnell's Designing Sound engine model assumes the exhaust gas through the valves is the main contribution, not sealed-chamber combustion; each cylinder adds a positive half-cosine every two cycles into a 4-quadrant feedback delay chain plus FM/waveshaping; Baldan judges it lacks higher harmonics and is hard to control.
verdicts.evidence: Baldan Sec 2 states each of these points: exhaust gas is the 'salient acoustic contribution'; ignition matters less because it happens in 'perfectly sealed combustion chambers'; each cylinder contributes the 'positive half cycle of a cosine wave, once every two full cycles' into 'a delay chain with feedback, split in four quadrants'; the timbre is 'poor in higher order harmonics'; FM and waveshaping make it 'quite difficult to master, often with unnatural and hardly predictable acoustic results'. The aspress Practical 22 page agrees: 'engine pulse piston model (exhaust side) ... four stroke model with transmission, waveguide models of exhaust and body'. Farnell's book text itself was not checked.

verdicts.claim: Farnell Practical 22 Pd files (toy_boat_engine.pd, pulse_demo.pd, jitter_engine.pd, waveguide_engine.pd 'warped waveguide') published on aspress.co.uk with no licence; treat as all-rights-reserved, ideas only.
verdicts.evidence: The practical22 page lists those four files plus engines.wav ('warped waveguide engine algorithm'). Neither practical22.html nor the /sd/ index carries a licence statement. I also downloaded the site's examples.tar.gz (557 entries). It has no LICENSE, COPYING or README licence file, and grepping all .pd and .txt files found no licence or copyright text. Copyright with no licence means all rights reserved by default. The tarball's engine patches have different names (BOOK-PUREDATA/ENGINES/engine001.pd, four-stroke-engine.pd, fm-window-engine.pd and others), so there are two sets of files.

verdicts.claim: Antonio-R1/engine-sound-generator is MIT JS/Web Audio based on Baldan 2015; v1 (AudioBufferSourceNode.start) misbehaved in some browsers; v2 AudioWorklet; C++/Emscripten WASM port 'more efficient' and removed glitches.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub API reports the licence as MIT. README: 'based on the ideas from this paper' (Baldan, DOI 10.1109/SIVE.2015.7361287). On v1: 'does not seem to work correctly in some browsers'. On v2: 'uses an AudioWorklet'. The WASM port was made 'for making the sound generator more efficient and removing the glitches'. The WASM demo URL returns HTTP 200. But it is an incomplete Baldan implementation (see missed items). The throttle AudioParam is read but never used, there is no backfire, and it was last pushed 2022-11-06.

verdicts.claim: ange-yaghi/engine-sim is MIT; 10 kHz default sim; delayed per-cylinder exhaust flow to synth per exhaust system; delay=(header primary+exhaust length)/343, scaled by 1/length²; synth adds jitter/noise, DC block, IR convolution capped 10,000 samples, lowpass, leveler; Windows-only; author calls code 'sloppy'; moved to a community edition no longer actively maintained.
verdicts.evidence: The LICENSE file is MIT, (c) 2022 Ange Yaghi. simulator.cpp sets m_simulationFrequency=10000, and objects.mr defaults simulation_frequency to 10000, which an engine script can override. piston_engine_simulator.cpp computes delay=(headerPrimaryLength+exhaust->getLength())/343 m/s through a delay filter, then adds the result to each exhaust system's buffer multiplied by 1/(exhaustLength²). That 1/length² factor scales the amplitude, not the delay. synthesizer.cpp limits IR taps to min(10000, last sample with |IR| above 100). The render path is: jitter filter, then subtraction of a 10 Hz lowpass (DC block), then multiplication by lowpassed air noise (multiplicative, not additive), then a derivative mix (dF_F_mix=0.01), then convolution, then a lowpass at 0.45·fs, then the leveler. The README states 'Note: this project currently only builds on Windows!' and has an FAQ heading 'Why is the code so sloppy?'. It also says 'Engine Simulator has moved!' and links to the community edition, whose README says it 'is no longer actively maintained as it is being replaced by a newer and more capable version'.

verdicts.claim: EngineLab (zolaski333, MIT, C++20/JUCE) derives exhaust sound from simulated pressure through a quasi-1D duct/waveguide network; README says V8/V12 may fall below real time on modest CPUs; therefore full gas-dynamic sim is too heavy for Tesla MCU2 browser.
verdicts.evidence: The factual parts are confirmed. The licence is MIT (GitHub API, LICENSE.md) and the code is 'Written in C++20 with JUCE'. The README says: 'the exhaust sound is the pressure actually computed at the valves, propagated through a quasi-1-D duct network'; 'characteristic waveguides'; 'Large engines (V8, V12) can fall below real time on a modest CPU'. However, the conclusion about Tesla MCU2 is an unverified inference: the README talks about desktop Windows CPUs running native C++, and no browser or WASM benchmark exists. It is plausible but has not been measured.

verdicts.claim: SDT (with the Baldan/Delle Monache combustion-engine model) is GPLv3-or-later; code cannot go into closed or permissively licensed Tesbox without copyleft obligations.
verdicts.evidence: LICENSE.txt: 'GNU General Public License ... either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later version'. AUTHORS.txt lists Stefano Baldan and Stefano Delle Monache. src/SDT/SDTMotor.h describes the same model: waveguides for intake pipes, cylinders, exhaust collectors, exhaust pipe, muffler and outlet, plus exhaust backfiring, and it also offers a two-stroke option. Shipping SDT-derived JS or WASM to browsers counts as conveying under the GPL, which triggers copyleft obligations.

verdicts.claim: PTR (Doerfler & Wyse, arXiv 2603.09391): sequential exhaust pulses; envelope E=(1-exp(-αφ))exp(-βφ) times decaying harmonic sum a_k∝e^(-0.5kλ); phase bending φ̃=2π(φ/2π)^ν; Karplus-Strong resonators; V8 firing order [1,5,4,8,6,3,7,2] with ±40° per-cylinder offsets.
verdicts.evidence: arXiv v2 (2 Jun 2026; to appear at EUSIPCO 2026) has Eq. 4 E_i=(1-exp(-α_i φ_i))exp(-β_i φ_i), Eq. 6 with a_{i,k}∝e^(-0.5kλ_i), and Eq. 5 φ̃=2π[φ/2π]^ν with ν∈(0,1]. Phase uses f0=RPM/120. The firing order is [1,5,4,8,6,3,7,2] with 'learned per-cylinder timing adjustments bounded to ±40° crank angle'. One error: the resonator topology is not 'two per bank'. Sec IV-C4 says 'Two independent resonators process cylinder bank outputs ... combined in a final shared resonator', which is one per bank, three in total (see the separate refuted entry).

verdicts.claim: PTR uses two Karplus-Strong resonators per bank plus one shared resonator.
verdicts.evidence: Sec IV-C4: 'Two independent resonators process cylinder bank outputs (modeling distinct manifold paths), with processed signals combined in a final shared resonator (common exhaust pipe).' That is one resonator per bank (cylinders 1–4 left, 5–8 right) plus one shared, three in total. The resonators are fixed (not time-varying) learned parameters. Each uses y[n]=x[n]+g·(α·y[n-L]+β·y[n-L-1]).

verdicts.claim: PTR gating: g_thr=max(torque,ε)^0.7 (ε=0.02), DFCO=max(-torque,ε); turbulence = AM of pulses × g_thr; separate airflow noise in fuel cut; beat HPN baseline by 21% harmonic reconstruction (5.7% total loss); trained at 16 kHz.
verdicts.evidence: Eq. 1 is g_thr=max(torque,ε)^0.7 with ε=0.02, and Eq. 2 is g_DFCO=max(-torque,ε). Eq. 7 is P̂=P·[1+α_turb·g_thr·η]+η·[E(φ)·g_thr+g_DFCO], which includes an extra throttle-gated, cycle-synchronous intake-pulsation noise term the claim omits. The audio rate is 16 kHz. Correction: 5.7% is the mean reduction in total loss, not the loss value. The per-dataset improvement is 3.8–7.6%, plus 21% better harmonic reconstruction. The torque units/scaling in g_thr are not stated in the text, so ε=0.02 cannot be mapped to Nm with confidence.

verdicts.claim: PTR code and weights are CC BY-NC 4.0; Procedural Engine Sounds dataset is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; neither usable commercially; only ideas reimplementable.
verdicts.evidence: PTR README: 'licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC 4.0)', with 'For commercial use, please contact the author' (so a commercial licence may be negotiable). The non-commercial conclusion holds for both code and data. However, the dataset licence is wrong in the claim: Zenodo and Hugging Face both list the dataset as CC BY-NC 4.0, with no ShareAlike. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is the arXiv licence of the paper texts (2603.07584 and 2603.09391). See the separate refuted entry.

verdicts.claim: The Procedural Engine Sounds dataset is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
verdicts.evidence: The Zenodo record 16883336 metadata gives license id 'cc-by-nc-4.0', and its description says 'License: CC BY-NC 4.0'. The Hugging Face dataset card says license: cc-by-nc-4.0. The BY-NC-SA 4.0 the researcher saw is the arXiv paper's licence ('License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0' on arxiv.org/html/2603.07584v1), not the dataset's.

verdicts.claim: Order-based synthesis is the standard ASD method; neosonic authors (Bodden & Belschner) say it is 'rigid and idealized', neglects firing-to-firing micro-variation that must be added for natural sound; heavy character changes (I4→V8) sound artificial.
verdicts.evidence: Inter-noise 2014 p467 (Bodden & Belschner, neosonic). Quotes: 'The standard sound synthesis method to support combustion engine sound is the order based synthesis'; the gain is 'controlled by the engine load and/or the pedal position'; 'the order based approach is a kind of rigid and idealized implementation ... neglecting the micro structure ... the cylinder firings are never completely identical'; micro-structure variations are overlaid 'resulting in more natural sounds'; 'change an I4 engine to a V6 or V8 ... mostly result in artificial sounds which also usually do not fit to the vehicle itself'. Caveats: the paper is from 2014 and concerns augmenting a running combustion engine. Wikipedia's ASD article says 'there is no one unified model'. The 'does not fit the vehicle' argument partly assumes a real engine is audible underneath, which a Tesla does not have.

corrections: engine-sim: the 1/exhaustLength² factor scales the amplitude of each cylinder's contribution, not the delay. The value written is not a mass flow either. It is exhaust-runner gauge pressure (p − 1 atm) plus 0.1× two dynamic-pressure terms, multiplied by 1600 × attenuation³. attenuation = min(|engine speed|,40)/40, which fades the sound near standstill. It is then scaled by per-cylinder sound attenuation, the exhaust system's audio volume and 1/cylinderCount. (src/piston_engine_simulator.cpp)

engine-sim synthesizer: noise is multiplicative (the signal is multiplied by lowpassed air noise, airNoise=1.0, cutoff 2 kHz), not additive. Each input channel is lowpassed at 1.9 kHz before convolution, so the high band comes from the IR. Defaults: dF_F_mix=0.01, leveler target 30000, max gain 1.9, input jitter 0.5 with a 10 kHz cutoff. (synthesizer.cpp/.h)

engine-sim convolution is direct time-domain FIR, O(N) per sample. Up to 10,000 taps per exhaust channel at 44.1 kHz is about 441M MAC/s per channel, far too heavy for a browser as written. A port would need FFT or partitioned convolution (e.g., Web Audio ConvolverNode).

engine-sim 'moved to a community edition': the CE repo is binary-only (Windows v0.1.14a, no source, no licence file). The author says the new Engine Simulator is not open source and is headed for a paid Steam release. The only MIT source is ange-yaghi/engine-sim, last pushed 2024-06-17.
'Sloppy' comes from the README's own FAQ heading 'Why is the code so sloppy?'. The author answers that it was written to demo in a YouTube video, not as a real product.
PTR resonators: one Karplus-Strong resonator per bank (two in total) plus one shared resonator, not two per bank.
PTR results: 5.7% is the mean reduction in total validation loss versus HPN (3.8–7.6% per dataset), not the total loss itself. 21% is the improvement in harmonic reconstruction.

The Procedural Engine Sounds dataset is CC BY-NC 4.0 (Zenodo/HF), not CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. BY-NC-SA 4.0 is the arXiv licence of both Doerfler & Wyse paper texts. The PTR README invites commercial-licence enquiries ('For commercial use, please contact the author').

Baldan's printed ignition equation s(x)=sin(2π(xt+0.5)), 0<x<t, conflicts with the text. It is negative for small x and sits at the cycle start, inside the intake window 0–0.25. The text says it is a positive half-sine at the start of the expansion phase (about x=0.5 in the paper's own convention: intake 0–0.25, exhaust 0.75–1, piston TDC at x=0, 0.5, 1). An implementer must choose the ignition phase deliberately rather than copy the printed formula.

Baldan backfire: repeated squaring gives p^(2^n) after n backfires. That is doubly exponential in the backfire count, although the paper calls it 'exponential'. No reset rule is given, and the authors flag the backfire algorithm as needing improvement.
EngineLab: the 'too heavy for MCU2' conclusion is an inference. The README only says V8/V12 can drop below real time on a modest (desktop Windows) CPU in native C++.

Farnell examples: the site's examples.tar.gz names its engine patches BOOK-PUREDATA/ENGINES/engine001-003.pd, four-stroke-engine.pd, fm-window-engine.pd, phase-position-shaping.pd and others. These differ from the Practical 22 page's toy_boat_engine.pd / pulse_demo.pd / jitter_engine.pd / waveguide_engine.pd, so two file sets exist. Neither has a licence.

Bodden & Belschner (2014) call order synthesis 'the standard' for supporting a running combustion engine. Wikipedia's ASD article says there is 'no one unified model'. Industry alternatives exist, e.g., GeneCars uses additive synthesis of Bark-scale partials (described in Baldan Sec 2), and Harman's patents cover sample-based approaches.
missed: Antonio-R1 implementation gaps (read from source). The throttle AudioParam is copied into this.throttle but never used, so ignition amplitude is fixed (pistonMotion×1.5 + fuelIgnition×5.0). There is no backfire. Filter coefficients hard-code SAMPLING_RATE=44100 in both JS and C++, and waveguide lengths are passed in samples, so resonances shift about 8.8% at a 48 kHz AudioContext unless rescaled. Cylinders are evenly spaced at i/N of the cycle plus one shared lowpassed random crank jitter, so there is no firing order and no uneven-firing (cross-plane V8, boxer) modelling. Ignition is sin(2πx/t) on 0<x<0.5t, i.e., at the cycle start. The last push was 2022-11-06. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Antonio-R1/engine-sound-generator/main/src/engine_sound_generator/engine_sound_generator_worklet.js and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Antonio-R1/engine-sound-generator/main/src/engine_sound_generator/sound_generator_wasm/engine_sound_generator.cpp

Baldan control set (useful as a Tesbox parameter schema). Cylinders: 1–12, cc, compression ratio, ignition time 0–1, cycle asymmetry 0–1, engine-block gain. Intakes: average length in m, gain. Extractors: average length. Exhaust main pipe length. Muffler: average length and action 0–1. Outlet: length and gain. RPM. Throttle 0 (idle) to 1. Piston motion modulates the cylinder waveguide delay. The validation was informal only: compared with a recording at about 900 RPM idle, the synthetic sound had less mid/high energy. https://air.iuav.it/bitstream/11578/264484/1/SIVE15_submission_4.pdf

SDT's SDTMotor.h is the open GPLv3+ implementation of the Baldan model, by the same authors. It exposes backfire chance [0,1], muffler size/feedback and a two-stroke option. Reading it while reimplementing creates copyleft-contamination risk, so a clean implementation should work from the paper only. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SkAT-VG/SDT/main/src/SDT/SDTMotor.h

PTR was trained and validated only on the Procedural Engine Sounds dataset. That dataset is synthetic: an analysis-driven extended harmonic-plus-noise synthesizer driven by 5–10 min of real audio per engine, augmented 15–30×. So the 21%/5.7% gains over an HPN baseline are measured on HPN-generated data, not real recordings. All time-varying PTR parameters are network-predicted, so a non-neural Tesbox would have to hand-tune them. The model uses a fixed V8 firing-order prior even on the inline-4 subset. 16 kHz training limits bandwidth to 8 kHz. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07584 , https://arxiv.org/html/2603.09391

Dataset facts: 5,935 files, about 19.01 h, 48 kHz 4-channel WAV (stereo audio plus RPM×1e-4 and torque Nm×1e-3 encoded as audio channels), CC BY-NC 4.0, published 2025-08-21. https://zenodo.org/records/16883336

EngineLab details. It is Windows-only and self-described as 'early': the sound 'is not there yet', and engines are 'recognisable by their cylinder count and firing rhythm, but not yet as a specific engine'. Gas-solver cells are about 0.36 m. It depends on JUCE, which is dual AGPLv3/commercial (JUCE 9 licence). Its exhaust IRs in assets/ir/ come from engine-sim under MIT (©2022 Ange Yaghi), so those IRs are a usable permissive asset if their provenance holds. The repo was created 2026-07-03 and has 1 star. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zolaski333/EngineLab/main/README.md , https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juce-framework/JUCE/master/LICENSE.md

DasEtwas/enginesound verified as MIT, Rust, 'loosely based on' the Baldan paper. It is a GUI/CLI offline WAV generator with crossfade-loop export, not a web runtime. Last push 2023-06-06. https://github.com/DasEtwas/enginesound

Harman patents verified on Google Patents. US12243510B2 'Methods and systems for engine sound synthesis' (Harman International): priority 2021-10-28, granted 2025-03-04, adjusted expiration 2043-07-08, Active. US9553553B2 'Engine sound synthesis system' (Harman Becker): priority 2012-07-12, granted 2017-01-24, adjusted expiration 2035-03-16, Active. 'Active' is Google's status, not a legal opinion. https://patents.google.com/patent/US12243510B2/en , https://patents.google.com/patent/US9553553B2/en

Baldan cites US 6,959,094 (Cascone et al., 2005, 'Apparatus and methods for synthesis of internal combustion engine vehicle sounds') as patented physically-informed engine synthesis prior art. Its status was not checked here; it is likely expired given its age, but this should be confirmed before freedom-to-operate sign-off. https://air.iuav.it/bitstream/11578/264484/1/SIVE15_submission_4.pdf

Baldan's paper says its three outputs (intake, engine block, exhaust) are meant for dynamic listening-point rendering (interior/exterior/front/rear). This maps directly onto Tesbox's cabin vs exterior perspective feature: mix the block-vibration and intake outputs for cabin, and the outlet for exterior. https://air.iuav.it/bitstream/11578/264484/1/SIVE15_submission_4.pdf

research.summary:
Research covered how to turn GPS speed into engine RPM and load, and the published specs for a starter garage. Clean-room rule was kept: nothing from rupteur.app was searched, opened or read. The session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out partway through, so the later items were checked with direct fetches of primary documents.

RPM formula: rpm = v / C_dyn × overall_ratio × 60. C_dyn is π × unloaded diameter × about 0.97. The unloaded diameter is 2 × width × aspect/100 + rim × 25.4 mm. The 0.97 factor was checked against EPA "N/V" (rpm per mph in top gear) for five real cars. It matched within 0–1.3%: RS3 29.2/29.2, M3 6MT 37.8/37.7, M3 8AT 26.0/26.1, AMG GT63 23.9/24.2, Civic Type R 38.7/38.6. Some dual-clutch gearboxes, such as the RS3 7-speed S tronic and the R8, use two final-drive ratios. So the app should store the overall ratio for each gear.

Load estimation: the EPA 2025/2026 Test Car List gives per-Tesla road-load coefficients A/B/C plus test weight and rated hp. That allows F_road(v) = A + Bv + Cv². Throttle can then be estimated as (m·a + F_road) / F_max(v), where F_max = min(m·a_launch, P/v).

GPS speed: the W3C spec says coords.speed is in m/s and may be null, and browsers may rate-limit updates. A typical GNSS receiver measures velocity from Doppler to about 0.05 m/s, far better than differencing positions accurate to about 2.5 m. Recommended chain: coords.speed first, then a Kalman filter on speed and acceleration, then a forward prediction using position.timestamp, a standstill deadband with hysteresis, and a decay model when the signal drops out.

Tesla browser: it is Chromium on Linux, with Chromium 79 and 88 seen in 2020–2022 user-agent strings, and AudioWorklet has been in Chrome since version 66. Geolocation works and apps say it uses the car's GPS. Developer reports conflict: one app polls every 4 s because watchPosition crashed the tab, another uses watchPosition. DeviceMotion is doubtful: Chromium on Linux needs kernel-exposed (IIO) sensors, and orientation events were reported to crash the browser.

Shift logic: separate upshift and downshift curves with a 10–40% gap. Shifts take about 80–200 ms. A torque converter multiplies torque 1.8–2.5× at stall, couples at about 90% speed ratio, and locks up at roughly 900–1700 rpm. Idle is typically 600–1000 rpm.

Garage specs (all from manufacturer sheets except the LFA gear ratios): RS3, 911 GT3, M3 G80, AMG GT 63, Civic Type R FL5, Lexus LFA, and Audi R8 V10 as the official-data alternative.

claims.claim: Engine RPM = v[m/s] / C_dyn[m] * (gear_ratio * final_drive) * 60; equivalently rpm per km/h = overall_ratio / C_dyn * 1000/60. Standard US forms: rpm = mph * ratio * 336 / tyre_diameter_in.

ISO metric tyre code 245/35 R19: 245 = section width mm, 35 = sidewall height as % of width, R = radial, 19 = rim diameter in inches. Unloaded diameter mm = 2*width*aspect/100 + rim*25.4 (245/35R19 -> 654.1 mm).

Loaded (rolling) radius is smaller than unloaded radius: r_static < r_dyn < r_0. Common practice multiplies unloaded diameter by a rolling factor of about 0.96-0.98 (0.97 typical default); mechguru uses SLR = 0.96*R.

DERIVED VALIDATION: using C_dyn = pi*D_unloaded*0.97 with manufacturer gear/final-drive ratios and the driven (rear) tyre reproduces the EPA-published top-gear N/V ratio (rpm per mph) within 0-1.3%: Audi RS3 29.2 vs EPA 29.2; BMW M3 6MT 37.8 vs 37.7; M3 Comp 8AT 26.0 vs 26.1; AMG GT63 23.9 vs 24.2; Civic Type R 38.7 vs 38.6. So 0.97 is a good default factor.

The EPA Test Car List (xlsx, 2017-2026) gives for every tested vehicle: Equivalent Test Weight, Rated HP, # gears, Axle Ratio, N/V Ratio, and road-load Target Coefficients A (lbf), B (lbf/mph), C (lbf/mph^2). Road-load force F = A + B*v + C*v^2. This is a public primary dataset usable for both Tesla resistance modelling and ICE gearing cross-checks.

EPA 2026 Tesla road-load data (ETW lb; A lbf; B lbf/mph; C lbf/mph^2; rated hp): Model 3 Standard RWD 18in 4000; 27.99; 0.1172; 0.01335; 305 hp. Model 3 Long Range AWD 4250; 30.98; 0.1596; 0.01410; 397 hp. Model 3 Performance 4250; 36.82; 0.1386; 0.01545; 510 hp. Model S Long Range 4750; 26.37; 0.3082; 0.01390; 658 hp. Model S Plaid 5000; 32.10; 0.3202; 0.01396; 1006 hp. Model X Plaid 5500; 31.45; 0.3973; 0.01620; 925 hp. Cybertruck AWD 7000; 38.64; 0.4110; 0.02650; 621 hp. DERIVED: speed from differencing two 1 Hz positions has noise of about sqrt(2)*sigma_pos/dt, roughly 3.5 m/s (about 12.7 km/h) at sigma 2.5 m. It is also lagged by about dt/2 (an average over the last interval). Doppler speed (coords.speed) is roughly 70x less noisy, so position differencing should only be a long-baseline (5-25 s) fallback when speed is null, as TeslaRadar does (~24 s net displacement).
Many browsers return coords.speed = null, so apps fall back to Haversine differencing of consecutive fixes (example: enableHighAccuracy:true, maximumAge:1000, timeout:10000).

Alpha-beta filter: predict x += dt*v; residual r = z - x; correct x += alpha*r and v += (beta/dt)*r. Stable for 0<alpha<1 and 0<beta<=2, but noise is suppressed only for beta<1. It equals a steady-state Kalman filter when the gains come from process and measurement noise. Suits a speed+acceleration state with speed measurements at 1-10 Hz.

The 1-euro filter (Casiez, Roussel, Vogel, CHI 2012) is a low-pass filter with adaptive cutoff = mincutoff + beta*|dx/dt|. Low cutoff kills jitter when slow or stationary, higher cutoff cuts lag when moving fast. Tuning: beta=0, set mincutoff to remove jitter, then raise beta to remove lag. BSD/MIT implementations exist, including JS/TS. Good for stationary jitter with low lag.

Shift schedules map vehicle speed against throttle or load. Upshift points come from where adjacent-gear acceleration curves intersect (max-performance) or from a BSFC optimum (economy), computed at 20/40/60/80/100% throttle. Downshift curves are offset by a buffer B (typically 10-40%): v_down(n+1) = (1-B)*v_up(n). This prevents gear hunting.

Hysteresis between upshift and downshift is classic shift-valve behaviour: the downshift occurs at a considerably lower speed than the upshift, and both lines move to higher speeds as throttle opening increases.

Kickdown is triggered when throttle (or accelerator/target torque) exceeds a high threshold near wide-open throttle. Throttle rate also sets aggressiveness: a fast pedal application gives a quick, aggressive kickdown, a slow one gives a gentler downshift.

Shift durations: ZF 8HP about 200 ms (performance calibrations 50-160 ms). Porsche PDK under 100 ms (911 7-speed), about 80 ms (Panamera 8-speed). Lexus LFA ASG 150-200 ms. A skilled human manual shift takes about 200-400 ms. DCT/PDK upshifts have no traction interruption.

Rev matching on downshift: a throttle blip raises engine speed to the new gear's input-shaft speed (= v * new overall ratio / C_dyn * 60). Mismatch causes driveline shock. Automatic rev-match has been on production manuals since Nissan in 2009 and is now near-universal (Civic Type R 6MT has Rev-Match Control).

Torque converter: stall torque multiplication is 1.8:1 to 2.5:1 for most cars. Coupling is reached at a turbine/impeller speed ratio of about 0.9, where lock-up is usually applied. The K-factor (Np/sqrt(Tp)) is nearly constant from stall to about 0.6 speed ratio, then rises rapidly. Impeller torque is about Np^2/K^2.

Lock-up practice (LuK/Schaeffler): 1990s 4-speeds locked in 3rd/4th between 1,100 and 1,700 rpm. Modern strategies lock up in all gears down to about 900 rpm, with controlled continuous slip at low rpm or high load and modulated slip during shifts and tip-ins. The ZF 8HP converter is reportedly locked in gears 2-8 (open, slip, lock modes).
Passenger-car idle speed is customarily 600-1000 rpm and is raised under accessory load (A/C). Engines tuned for high-rpm power tend to idle roughly unless idle is raised.

Launch control holds engine rpm at a set value before the clutch is engaged by the computer or the driver. It applies only to clutch-type gearboxes (manual or DCT). Aftermarket 'two-step' limiters use a launch rpm cap plus a normal rev limit.

Firing orders: inline-4 1-3-4-2; inline-5 1-2-4-5-3; inline-6 1-5-3-6-2-4; flat-6 R1-L3-R2-L1-R3-L2 (or R1-L2-R3-L1-R2-L3). Four-stroke firing interval = 720 deg / n (I5 144 deg, I6 120 deg, V10 even-fire 72 deg). Uneven intervals give burble or growl.

recommendations: Store each car as per-gear OVERALL ratios (gear x final drive), not gear plus one final drive. The RS3 and R8 dual-clutch gearboxes use two final drives. Compute C_dyn = pi * (2*w*ar/100 + rim*25.4)/1000 * 0.97 from the driven-axle tyre (rear on staggered cars). Unit-test it against the EPA N/V values (RS3 29.2, M3 6MT 37.7, M3 8AT 26.1, AMG GT63 24.2, Civic Type R 38.6), aiming for within 2%.

Speed pipeline: (1) prefer coords.speed. If it is null, use long-baseline displacement (5-25 s) only as a fallback, never single 1 s hops. (2) Run a 2-state Kalman or alpha-beta filter on [v, a], with measurement variance scaled by coords.accuracy and staleness. (3) Predict forward to performance.now() using position.timestamp, so a 1 Hz feed still drives 60 Hz audio. Cap extrapolation at about 1.5-2 s. (4) Hold at zero with hysteresis below about 0.5-1 m/s (enter at 0.5, leave at 1.0) or use a 1-euro filter, so idle doesn't jitter at stoplights. (5) On dropouts or tunnels, keep extrapolating while decaying acceleration toward the coast-down deceleration -F_road(v)/m. After about 5 s with no fix, fade into a neutral cruise at constant speed and low load, and show a 'GPS lost' state.

Measure on a real car before locking design: geolocation fix rate, how often coords.speed is null, latency (Date.now() - position.timestamp), and whether watchPosition is stable or crashes. Build both a watchPosition path and a getCurrentPosition polling path, selectable by feature flag. Also test while Tesla Navigation is active, given the 2023 ABRP bug.

Load estimation: F_req = m*a_filtered + F_road(v), with F_road = A + B*v + C*v^2 from the EPA coefficients for the chosen Tesla. Use F_max(v) = min(m*a_launch, eta*P_rated/v), with a_launch from 0-60 (Model 3 RWD about 4.6 m/s^2, Plaid about 13.5). Load = clamp(F_req/F_max, 0, 1). This automatically makes a slow Tesla reach full throttle sooner than a Plaid. Negative F_req maps to overrun/engine braking. Below the coast-down deceleration, treat it as braking or regen with zero throttle. Low-pass the load (about 150-300 ms) and apply a light deadband.

Do not compute grade from GPS altitude by default; it is too noisy. Optionally add a slowly-adapting bias on the load estimate, because a 5% grade equals about 0.05 g, which is 10% of a Model 3 RWD's full-throttle force.

Automatic shift logic: build upshift-rpm curves as a function of load. Example: about 0.30*redline at light load rising to about 0.97*redline at WOT in sport mode. Economy mode uses lower points. Downshift line = (1-B)*upshift with B of about 0.15-0.30 in speed terms. Add a minimum time in gear (about 1-2 s), kickdown when load > 0.9 and its rate of change is high (go down 1-2 gears if the target rpm stays under redline), and coast downshifts when rpm falls below about 1.2-1.5k. Model shift time of about 80-200 ms (DCT/PDK ~100 ms, 8-speed TC ~200 ms) with a brief torque/load dip on upshift. On downshift, blip to the new-gear sync rpm before engaging.

Torque-converter cars (e.g. M3 Competition 8AT): engine rpm = max(turbine rpm / speed ratio, stall-curve rpm as a function of load), blending into lock-up at a speed ratio of about 0.9. Lock up from 2nd gear above about 1,100-1,700 rpm (down to about 900 in modern units). Allow slip of a few tens of rpm under high load, and unlock on kickdown. Stall rpm should rise with load (for example idle +600 to +1,500 at WOT).

Clutch-type launch (manual or DCT) from standstill: engine rpm = idle + load*(launch_rpm - idle), floored by wheel-derived rpm. Taper clutch slip over about 0.5-1.0 s, or until wheel-derived rpm reaches engine rpm, then lock. Launch rpm is roughly 3-4.5k for turbo cars and 5-6k for high-revving NA engines (tunable, not manufacturer data).

Manual mode: never let it stall. Below about idle-equivalent speed (about 6-9 km/h in 1st), auto-disengage the clutch and idle. Offer an optional auto-downshift when rpm drops below about 1,000-1,200. Block or warn on downshifts whose sync rpm would exceed redline (prevent money-shifts). Run a bouncing rev limiter at redline. Auto rev-match on button downshifts.

Idle: base 700-900 rpm by engine (high-revving NA engines toward the upper end). Add small random fluctuation (±10-30 rpm) plus a raised cold-start idle for the first ~30-60 s for realism. The 600-1000 rpm range is documented; per-engine idle values are not published.

Pick sonically distinct firing patterns for the garage: I5 1-2-4-5-3 (RS3), flat-6 even 120 deg (GT3), I6 1-5-3-6-2-4 (M3), cross-plane V8 uneven per bank (AMG GT 63 C192; avoid the 2026 M177 Evo and the Black Series, which are flat-plane), I4 1-3-4-2 (Civic Type R), even-fire 72 deg V10 (LFA). Optionally add the odd-fire 90/54 deg R8/Huracán V10 as a contrast. Use the R8's official ratios if the LFA ratios can't be verified.

Treat DeviceMotion as an optional enhancer only. Feature-detect it, listen for about 2 s, and use it only if events arrive with non-zero, plausible longitudinal acceleration. Never use DeviceOrientation (reported to crash Tesla Chromium). If it is available, fuse it as a high-rate acceleration input in the Kalman filter with GPS speed as the low-rate absolute reference, and estimate mounting axis and bias online.

Demo mode should reuse the same physics: integrate a = (F_drive(load) - F_road(v))/m for the selected Tesla with scripted pedal inputs. It then exercises the identical RPM, load and shift code path without GPS.

Is the browser's geolocation fused with Tesla's IMU and wheel odometry (dead-reckoning that keeps updating in tunnels), or raw GNSS that stops?
What Chromium version does the 2025-2026 Tesla browser run? No public UA string newer than Chromium 88 (2022) was found, and the WebSearch budget ran out before more checks could be made.
