Per-engine idle rpm and launch-control rpm are not in the manufacturer sheets that were retrieved; values will be design choices within the documented 600-1000 rpm idle range.
Which Tesla trims lack a subwoofer (Model 3 Standard / RWD Highland, Model Y Standard 7-speaker)? This needs confirmation from Tesla owner's manuals.

verdicts.claim: Engine RPM = v[m/s] / C_dyn[m] * (gear_ratio * final_drive) * 60; rpm per km/h = overall_ratio / C_dyn * 1000/60; US form rpm = mph * ratio * 336 / tyre_diameter_in.
verdicts.evidence: Checked the kinematics myself. 1 mph = 1056 in/min, and 1056/π = 336.1, so rpm = mph × ratio × 336/D_in. The m/s and km/h forms are the same relation. Real gearboxes break it in three cases: an unlocked torque converter, clutch slip at launch, and DCTs with two final drives. In those cases engine rpm is not kinematically tied to wheel speed.

verdicts.claim: ISO metric tyre code 245/35 R19 meanings; unloaded diameter mm = 2*width*aspect/100 + rim*25.4 (245/35R19 -> 654.1 mm).
verdicts.evidence: Wikipedia Tire code gives the formula (2×T×A/100)+(W×25.4) and calls the result the 'theoretical diameter'. Aspect ratio is sidewall height as a % of nominal section width. 2×245×0.35 + 19×25.4 = 654.1 mm. Caveat: real tyres differ from the nominal size by make, model and rim width.

verdicts.claim: r_static < r_dyn < r_0; rolling factor ~0.96-0.98 (0.97 typical); mechguru uses SLR = 0.96*R.
verdicts.evidence: German Wikipedia (Abrollumfang, citing Rill and DIN 70020) says the dynamic rolling radius is larger than the static loaded radius, with r_D ≈ 2/3·r0 + 1/3·r_S, and rolling circumference is measured at 60 km/h. The mechguru quote is accurate, but mechguru mixes up static loaded radius with rolling radius ('rolling radius or static loaded radius'). That is technically wrong, even though 0.96 happens to land near the empirical range. The same source says radial tyres grow about 1% at 180 km/h compared with 60 km/h. It also says 7 mm of tread wear changes rolling circumference by about 1.3–2%.

verdicts.claim: C_dyn = pi*D_unloaded*0.97 + manufacturer ratios + driven tyre reproduces EPA N/V within 0-1.3% (RS3 29.2/29.2, M3 6MT 37.8/37.7, M3 Comp 8AT 26.0/26.1, AMG GT63 23.9/24.2, Civic Type R 38.7/38.6).
verdicts.evidence: I re-downloaded the EPA 2025/2026 xlsx and the BMW, Audi and Honda documents and recomputed. BMW 09/2020 sheet: 6MT 6th 0.846, final drive 3.462; 8AT 8th 0.640, final drive 3.154; rear tyre 285/35ZR19. That gives 37.79 and 26.05, against EPA 37.7 and 26.1. Honda: 6th 0.734, final drive 3.842, 265/30R19, giving 38.69 against EPA 38.6. Caveats: (1) The EPA 37.7 row is the 'M4 Coupe' 6MT; no M3 6MT row exists in 2025/2026. (2) RS3: the Audi eTD lists one final drive, 4.059, and 7th 0.630, which gives 34.4. The 29.2 only comes out with EPA's axle ratio of 3.45, so this case used EPA input, not the manufacturer sheet. (3) The RS3 is a transverse quattro whose gearbox final drive turns the FRONT axle. Its front tyre is 265/30R19 (641.6 mm); the 245/35R19 is the rear. With the front tyre the result is 29.8, +2.1%. A realistic error band is about ±2%, not 0–1.3%. Even so, 0.97 is a sound default.

verdicts.claim: EPA Test Car List (xlsx 2017-2026) gives ETW, rated HP, #gears, axle ratio, N/V, target coefficients A/B/C; F = A + Bv + Cv^2; usable for Tesla resistance and ICE gearing.
verdicts.evidence: The 2026 file has 3,901 rows, all with Target Coef A/B/C, ETW, axle ratio, N/V and rated HP filled in. The page also offers CSV files for 2000–2016 and zip files back to 1984. Caveats: (a) 40 CFR 86.1803-01 defines N/V in top gear but lets the manufacturer use the 1:1 gear instead. One row looks like that: 2026 911 Carrera S Cabriolet shows N/V 39.0 while its siblings show 23.3. (b) ETW is an inertia class based on loaded vehicle weight = curb weight + 300 lb. (c) Use the Target coefficients, not the 'Set Coef' (dyno-setting) ones. (d) 733 of 3,901 rows have negative B, which is a curve-fit artifact. (e) For EVs the axle ratio is a 1.0 placeholder.

Every listed value matches the xlsx rows exactly. Caveat: the 2025 'Model Y Performance AWD' row (452 hp, 39.409/0.2207/0.0169) is identical to the MY2024 file. It is the carried-over pre-Juniper Performance, not the new Juniper Performance. The 2025 Model Y LR AWD row did change (37.77/-0.1538/0.02044), so that one is the new car. The 2026 file has no Model Y rows. Model 3 Performance values differ between 2025 (40.56/0.1527/0.0145) and 2026.

verdicts.claim: SI road-load at 100 km/h: 386 N (M3 Std RWD), 424 (M3 LR AWD), 467 (M3 Perf), 477 (MY LR AWD), 503 (MS Plaid 19in), 741 (Cybertruck AWD); A/(m g) Crr ~0.0055-0.0087; conversion factors.
verdicts.evidence: Recomputed: 386.2, 424.1, 467.4, 476.5 and 740.6 N. Exception: the 2026 Model S Plaid coefficients the researcher lists (32.10/0.3202/0.01396) give 471 N. The 503 N figure comes from the 2025 'Plaid (19" Wheels)' row (32.42/0.4783/0.0132). A/ETW ranges from 0.0055 (Model S LR, Cybertruck) to 0.0087 (M3 Perf). Conversion factors are right (B ×9.950, C ×22.258). Caveat: A is not pure rolling resistance (it also absorbs drivetrain and brake drag), and ETW is not real mass.

verdicts.claim: Tesla accel/mass: M3 2026 Std RWD 5.8 s 3,759 lb; Premium AWD 3.8 s 4,030 lb; Perf 2.9 s 4,054 lb; M3 Cd 0.219; MY 1,884-1,998 kg, LR AWD 0-60 4.8 s, Perf 0-100 3.5 s 2,033 kg, Cd 0.23; MS Plaid 1.98 s 760 kW Cd 0.208; MX Plaid 2.5 s 2,380 kg; Cybertruck RWD 6.2, AWD 4.1 @3,020 kg, Cyberbeast 2.6 @3,130 kg.
verdicts.evidence: Matches: M3 Cd 0.219; Plaid 1.98 s, 1,020 hp (760 kW), Cd 0.208; X Plaid 2.5 s and 5,248 lb (2,380 kg); Cybertruck 6.2/4.1/2.6 s; MY Cd 0.23; MY weight range 4,154–4,404 lb (1,884–1,998 kg); M3 base 3,759 lb (CarsDirect). Conflicts: (1) Wikipedia gives M3 Premium AWD 0–60 as 4.2 s, not 3.8 s. The researcher's own next claim also uses 4.2 s. (2) The Model Y '4.8 s' is Tesla Europe's 0–100 km/h figure, not 0–60 mph. (3) Wikipedia gives M3 Performance as 4,081 lb (Fremont), not 4,054. (4) Wikipedia gives MY Performance as 4,416 lb (2,003 kg), not 2,033 kg. (5) The Cybertruck masses are magazine-tested (MotorTrend 6,660 lb; C/D 6,901 lb), not Tesla figures. CarsDirect lists no 0–60 times. tesla.com returned 403, so I could not check against it.

verdicts.claim: Average 0-60 accel ≈0.47 g (M3 RWD), 0.65 (M3 LR 4.2 s), 0.94 (M3 Perf), 0.81 (MY Perf), 1.37 (Plaid), 0.67 (CT AWD), 1.05 (Cyberbeast); 5% grade ≈0.05 g ≈10% of M3 RWD capability.
verdicts.evidence: Recomputed: 0.472, 0.651, 0.943, 0.809 (0–100 km/h), 1.374–1.381, 0.667 and 1.052 g. sin(atan 0.05) = 0.0499 g, which is 10.6% of 0.472 g. Caveats: rollout-subtracted times overstate the average. Above roughly 50–60 km/h a Tesla is power-limited (a ≈ P/(m·v)), so at highway speed a grade takes a much larger share of the available acceleration than 10%.

verdicts.claim: W3C Geolocation CR Snapshot 26 Mar 2026: speed m/s or null; heading null (not NaN) when stationary; timestamp = acquisition time; watchPosition waits for significant change, UAs MAY rate-limit; updates stop when not visible; secure context + permission; enableHighAccuracy/timeout/maximumAge.
verdicts.evidence: Checked against the raw spec HTML. It is a 'W3C Candidate Recommendation Snapshot 26 March 2026'. The JSON section says heading is 'null if not available or the device is stationary', and the change log has 'Correction: Use null instead of NaN when stationary (#173)'. The spec contains 'User agents MAY impose a rate limit on how frequently position changes are reported' and 'If document is not fully active or visibility state is not "visible", go back ... wait'. Acquisition also waits while the document is hidden. MDN agrees on heading being null. Caveat: an automated WebFetch summary wrongly reported NaN, so I relied on the raw text. Browsers that predate #173 (Tesla shipped Chromium 75–88 in 2019–2022) may still return NaN, so code should accept null, NaN and non-finite values.

verdicts.claim: Tesla browser supports Geolocation API since firmware 5.9 with permission prompt; third-party apps report it reads car GPS continuously while driving.
verdicts.evidence: Main point confirmed: teslabrowserapps.com says it 'reads the car's GPS continuously', and two 2026 GitHub projects (TeslaRadar, VibeDrive) use navigator.geolocation in the Tesla browser. The 'since firmware 5.9' origin cannot be checked: forums.tesla.com does not resolve (ENOTFOUND), and the Wayback Machine has no copy of that thread.

verdicts.claim: TeslaRadar never uses watchPosition (crashed the tab), polls getCurrentPosition every 4 s with maximumAge ≤3 s; VibeDrive (Aug 2026, MIT) uses watchPosition({enableHighAccuracy:true}) and coords.speed.
verdicts.evidence: TeslaRadar repo (created 2026-09-10, no licence): src/lib/tesla-browser.ts reads '/** watchPosition + enableHighAccuracy has crashed Tesla Chromium. */'. constants.ts sets LOCATION_POLL_MS = 4000 and GEO_TESLA_MAXIMUM_AGE_MS = 3000, and also says '1 Hz JSON.stringify OOMs Qt Chromium'. The crash is blamed on watchPosition together with enableHighAccuracy, and the same app runs a heavy WebGL map, so the cause is confounded. VibeDrive (MIT, created 2026-08-20) does call watchPosition with {enableHighAccuracy:true, maximumAge:800}. It also polls getCurrentPosition every 1.5 s as a backup (enableHighAccuracy false, maximumAge 4 s). When coords.speed is not finite it falls back to haversine distance over time. So even the 'watchPosition' app does not rely on watchPosition alone.

verdicts.claim: AudioWorklet shipped in Chrome 66; GeolocationCoordinates.speed/heading in Chrome 5; Tesla Chromium ≥79 supports both.
verdicts.evidence: The BCD JSON fetched from GitHub gives AudioWorklet chrome 66, AudioWorkletNode 66, and GeolocationCoordinates.speed and .heading chrome 5. The interface was called 'Coordinates' in Chrome 5–78 and renamed in 79, which matters only for instanceof or name checks. Tesla user-agent strings also show Chromium 75 on 2019.36–2019.40 firmware, which is still above 66. AudioWorklet needs a secure context.

verdicts.claim: Tesla browser: video limited to Park; usable while driving only where Tesla permits; 2026.20 parental controls can disable browser.
verdicts.evidence: The 2026.20 release-note text (released 30 May 2026), quoted by NotATeslaApp, Tessie stats and tesla-info, reads: 'You can now block Browser, Theater, and Arcade from your Tesla by going to Controls > Safety > Parental Controls while in Park.' Video-in-Park-only comes from third-party sites only (teslabrowserapps). I could not reach the Tesla owner's manual (403). The regional rule is vague: codriver.io names no regions.

corrections: Model 3 Premium AWD 0-60 is 4.2 s on Wikipedia, not 3.8 s. The researcher's claim 9 also uses 4.2 s, so claims 8 and 9 contradict each other.
The Model Y '4.8 s' is Tesla Europe's 0-100 km/h figure for LR AWD, not 0-60 mph.

Model 3 Performance curb weight is 4,081 lb (Fremont) on Wikipedia, not 4,054 lb. Model Y Performance is 4,416 lb (2,003 kg), not 2,033 kg. Cybertruck masses of 3,020 and 3,130 kg are MotorTrend/Car and Driver test weights, not Tesla figures.

The 2025 EPA 'Model Y Performance AWD' road-load row (452 hp, 39.409/0.2207/0.0169) is identical to the MY2024 row. It is the legacy pre-Juniper car, so pairing it with Juniper Performance specs (0-100 3.5 s) mixes two generations.
The 503 N road load for the Model S Plaid uses the 2025 19-inch coefficients. The 2026 Plaid coefficients listed in claim 6 give 471 N.

RS3 N/V of 29.2 reproduces only with EPA's axle ratio of 3.45. Audi's eTD lists one final drive of 4.059, which with 7th gear 0.630 gives 34.4. The DCT uses two final drives, so take per-gear overall ratios from a reliable source rather than the eTD.

Transverse AWD cars (RS3, Golf R, other Haldex/MQB) drive the front axle through the gearbox final drive, so use the FRONT tyre. For the RS3 that is 265/30R19, which gives 29.8 instead of 29.2 (+2.1%). The 'driven (rear) tyre' rule only holds for longitudinal or RWD layouts.
The realistic validation error band is about ±2%, not 0-1.3%.

EPA N/V is not always top gear. 40 CFR 86.1803-01 lets the manufacturer use the 1:1 gear instead. The 2026 911 Carrera S Cabriolet row shows N/V 39.0 while the other 911 PDK rows show 23.3, so screen for outliers before using N/V for validation.
mechguru's 0.96 is a static loaded radius (SLR) factor that it wrongly treats as the rolling radius. The physics puts dynamic rolling radius between static and unloaded (r_D ≈ 2/3·r0 + 1/3·r_S).
EPA ETW is an inertia weight class based on loaded vehicle weight = curb weight + 300 lb. It is neither curb weight nor real mass, so A/ETW is only an approximate Crr.
The spec says heading is null when stationary, but Tesla's older Chromium (75/79/88 seen 2019-2022) predates spec change #173 and may return NaN. Treat null, NaN and non-finite values the same way.

TeslaRadar blames the crash on 'watchPosition + enableHighAccuracy' together, and the app also runs a heavy WebGL map, so the crash cause is confounded. VibeDrive runs watchPosition plus a 1.5 s getCurrentPosition backup poll, not watchPosition alone.
Tesla user-agent data shows Chromium 75 on 2019.36-2019.40 firmware, earlier than the 79/88 the researcher cites.
missed: Tesla 2026.26 (26 Jul 2026) raised the browser zoom level, and Tesla notes this can trigger a different (tablet/mobile) viewport on some sites. Design the layout for a smaller effective CSS viewport. The same update added cabin camera/mic access in the browser (camera only in Park). A secondary source (codriver.io, no citations) says the browser engine is now Chromium 148. That is not confirmed in the release notes.
Radial tyres grow about 1% in rolling circumference at 180 km/h versus 60 km/h, and tread wear shifts it about 1.3-2% (German Wikipedia, citing DIN 70020 and WdK 107). C_dyn is not constant.
Under DIN 70020, rolling circumference is defined at 60 km/h.

EPA road-load coefficients are tied to one wheel/tyre setup. Model 3 Standard RWD on 19-inch wheels needs about 422 N at 100 km/h versus 386 N on 18-inch (+9%). Plaid 21-inch rows also differ. Choosing the Tesla model alone does not pin down wheel size.
733 of 3,901 rows in the 2026 EPA file have a negative B coefficient. This is normal in coastdown fits, so do not reject or clamp it.

GPS-derived acceleration cannot see road grade, so a hill is indistinguishable from throttle. Whether coords.altitude is available in the Tesla browser was not checked, so separating grade from throttle is unresolved.

VibeDrive (MIT) describes itself as a recreation of the 'GPS cabin HUD' idea from dribe.app, which shows GPS-speed engine-sound apps for the Tesla browser already exist. The rupteur clean-room rule was respected; dribe.app was not opened.

With an automatic gearbox and an unlocked torque converter, or a manual during launch, engine rpm runs above the speed-derived rpm. The RPM model needs a slip state at low speed rather than pure kinematics.

research.summary:
Tesla data: the important split for Tesbox is whether the car has a subwoofer, not which model it is. Cars with no subwoofer: Model 3 Highland base RWD 2023-25 (9 speakers), Model Y RWD from about Jan 2024 (cut from 13 to 7 speakers), and Model 3/Y "Standard" from Oct 2025 (7 speakers). In these cars the 8-inch front-door woofers carry all the bass. A drop-in replacement woofer is rated 50 Hz-21 kHz and the 4-inch mids 95 Hz-21 kHz. Cars with a subwoofer: Model 3 LR/Premium/Performance (17 speakers, 2x8-inch subwoofers), Model Y Premium/Performance (15 speakers, 1x8-inch subwoofer), Cybertruck (15 speakers, 2 subwoofers), Model S/X (22 speakers, 960 W), Model Y L (19 speakers + subwoofer). Engine firing frequency is rpm x cylinders / 120, so idle fundamentals of about 27-47 Hz sit below what door woofers can play. Cars without a subwoofer need a high-pass filter plus added harmonics so the ear still hears the bass note ("virtual bass"); the main patent on this, US5930373, expired in 2017. Cabin gain (the car interior boosting bass below about 70-90 Hz) helps. The spec table below gives mass, power, 0-100 and top speed for each trim.

Legal: no rule found that bans synthetic engine sound inside the cabin. VW, BMW, Ford, Hyundai and Dodge all ship it. The real limits are: (1) do not touch the exterior pedestrian-warning speaker (US standard FMVSS 141; Tesla's Boombox recall 22V-068 made it Park-only); (2) in Germany the driver's hearing must not be impaired (StVO §23(1)), and touchscreen use while driving is limited to a brief glance (§23(1a)); the OLG Karlsruhe court fined a Tesla driver in 2020 for adjusting the wipers on the screen; (3) California bans stereo sound audible 50 ft or more outside the car (VC 27007).

Naming: Trademarkia shows no US or EU mark for TESBOX, and Tesla does not appear to own BOOMBOX. Other "Tes-" names for Tesla-related products are registered (TESSIE, TESMANIAN, TESERY). tesbox.com, .app, .de and .io are already registered by others. For engine names, generic descriptions are safest. Naming a brand only to refer to it is allowed if needed, minimal and without implied endorsement, but a synthesized sound is not the real car.

Competing products: Tesla-browser apps EV·ENGINE, Rombo and EV Sound FX; built into cars: Hyundai Ioniq 5 N (praised), Dodge Charger Daytona Fratzonic and BMW IconicSounds (mixed reviews). My WebSearch budget ran out partway, so some items below remain unverified.

claims.claim: Model 3 Highland base RWD (2023-2025; UK/EU review) has 9 speakers and NO subwoofer. Layout: three 100 mm dash mids; in each front door a 25 mm tweeter and a 200 mm (8") woofer; 100 mm mids in the rear doors. Tesla's website once listed a subwoofer for this trim in error.
Model 3 Highland AWD/Long Range has 17 speakers, including two 200 mm upward-firing subwoofers in the boot and dual 200 mm woofers in each front door.
2026 Model 3 Performance (North America) is listed with 15 speakers plus 2 subwoofers.

Model 3 Standard and Model Y Standard (launched 7 Oct 2025; US $36,990 / $39,990; also sold in Europe) have 7 speakers. The pricier versions have 15 speakers + 1 subwoofer. Standard trims also drop the rear screen, AM/FM radio and Autosteer (TACC only).

The Model Y 7-speaker standard system is 1 tweeter, 4 midranges, 2 woofers and 1 amp, with no subwoofer. The 15-speaker Premium system (Premium and Performance trims) is 3 tweeters, 9 mids, 2 woofers and 1 subwoofer (8", 160 W), with 2 amps (~560 W). Immersive Sound and a separate subwoofer level are Premium-only.

In about January 2024 the base Model Y RWD (US, pre-Juniper) was cut from 13 to 7 speakers: subwoofer removed, 2 amps reduced to 1, and the system renamed from 'Premium audio' to 'Custom audio'. Dual Motor and Performance kept premium audio.
Model Y L (6-seat, China from Sep 2025) has 19 speakers, a subwoofer and two extra overhead speakers; 340 kW, 2,088 kg, 0-60 mph 4.5 s (China).
Model S and Model X (2021+ refresh) have a 22-speaker, 960-watt audio system with Active Road Noise Reduction.
Cybertruck has 15 speakers, including 2 dedicated subwoofers (reported as 8" units under the rear bench), with distributed amplifiers.

Model 3 (2018-2024 and Highland), Model Y (2020-2025 and Juniper) and Cybertruck all use 8" (4 ohm) front-door woofers. A drop-in replacement (PowerBass OE8C-T3Y) is rated 50 Hz-21 kHz. The 4" dash/rear-door replacements are rated 95 Hz-21 kHz. Practical door-woofer bass floor is therefore about 50 Hz, and the rear 4" speakers should get no deep bass.
Car cabin gain adds roughly 12 dB/octave of bass reinforcement below a 'transfer frequency' of about 70-90 Hz. Smaller cabins get it at higher frequencies.
Car-audio practice for systems without a subwoofer is to high-pass door speakers around 60-80 Hz: about 80 Hz for 6.5" door mid-bass and about 60 Hz for 8" door woofers.

Four-stroke engine firing frequency is f = rpm x cylinders / 120 Hz, with harmonics at integer multiples. Examples: 4-cyl at 800 rpm = 26.7 Hz; 5-cyl at 850 rpm = 35 Hz; V8 at 700 rpm = 46.7 Hz. Idle fundamentals fall below the about 50 Hz door-woofer limit.

Virtual bass (the 'missing fundamental' effect): adding harmonics of frequencies below the speaker's cutoff makes listeners hear the low pitch through small speakers (Larsen & Aarts, JAES 50(3):147-164, 2002). Waves' MaxxBass patent US5930373 (priority 4 Apr 1997) expired 4 Apr 2017, so the technique is free to use.
Equal-loudness contours (ISO 226:2023, practically the same as 2003) show the ear loses low-frequency sensitivity at lower playback levels. This justifies volume-dependent bass compensation.
Car and Driver measured a Model 3 Highland Long Range RWD at 67 dB average at a 70 mph cruise, about 3 dB quieter than the pre-facelift car, thanks to acoustic-laminated glass all round.
WHO safe-listening weekly allowances: 80 dB for 40 h/week, 85 dB for 12.5 h, 90 dB for 4 h, 95 dB for 1 h 15 min, 100 dB for 20 min. WHO-ITU H.870 Mode 1 (adult) reference is 80 dBA for 40 h/week.

Tesla Boombox recall: Tesla recalled 578,607 US vehicles (2017-22 Model 3; 2020-22 Model S/X/Y) on 29 Jan 2022. Since firmware 2020.48.25, Boombox could play custom sounds through the pedestrian-warning speaker while moving, which could make the warning system non-compliant with FMVSS 141. Remedy: an OTA update disabling Boombox in Drive, Neutral and Reverse (Park-only).

FMVSS 141 (49 CFR 571.141) requires pedestrian alert sounds from stationary up to 30 km/h and in reverse. It bars any entity subject to NHTSA from disabling or altering the original-equipment sound system, or providing anyone a device intended to modify its sound-emitting capability. A cabin-only web app does not touch this system.

EU/UNECE R138 AVAS (exterior) operates up to 20 km/h and in reverse, at minimum 56 dB(A) at 20 km/h and maximum 75 dB(A) or the level of a comparable combustion car. It is mandatory for new types from 1 Jul 2019 and all new vehicles from 1 Jul 2021. Manufacturers may offer several driver-selectable sounds. UN R138 bans a pause switch; EU 540/2014 originally allowed one.

No rule was found that bans synthetic engine sound inside the cabin. Factory systems doing exactly this are on sale in the EU and US: VW Soundaktor (2011 Golf GTI/R), BMW Active Sound Design (F10 M5), Ford Active Noise Control (Mustang, F-150), Hyundai N Active Sound+ and BMW IconicSounds Electric.

Germany: StVO §23(1) makes the driver responsible for ensuring hearing is not impaired by 'Geräte' (devices). Music loud enough to impair hearing is a €10 warning fine. Failing to give way to an emergency vehicle is at least €240, 2 points and a 1-month ban.

OLG Karlsruhe (27 Mar 2020, 1 Rb 36 Ss 832/19) held that the built-in Tesla touchscreen is an 'electronic device' under StVO §23(1a). Using it while driving is allowed only with a brief glance suited to conditions, whatever the purpose. A driver adjusting wipers through a sub-menu got €200 and a 1-month ban.
UK Highway Code rule 148 says to avoid distractions 'such as loud music (this may mask other sounds)'. Rule 150 warns about distraction from in-vehicle multimedia systems.

California Vehicle Code 27007 bans operating a sound amplification system that can be heard 50 ft or more outside the vehicle on a highway (fine about $100-250). Very loud in-cabin playback with windows open could trigger it.

US nominative fair use (New Kids on the Block v. News America, 1992) allows using another's mark if (1) the product cannot readily be identified without it, (2) only as much of the mark as needed is used, and (3) nothing suggests sponsorship or endorsement. Example: an independent repair shop may advertise Volkswagen repairs if it implies no affiliation.

In the UK (and in the parallel EU provision, EUTMR Art. 14(1)(c), not fetched directly), a mark is not infringed by using it 'for the purpose of identifying or referring to goods or services as those of the proprietor', provided this follows 'honest practices in industrial or commercial matters'.

Jack Daniel's v. VIP Products (US Supreme Court, 2023): the Rogers expressive-use defence does not apply when the accused party uses the mark as a source designation for its own goods. Branding a preset or product with a car maker's mark gets weaker protection than descriptive reference.

Harley-Davidson tried to register its V-twin exhaust sound as a trademark (filed 1994). Nine competitors opposed and Harley withdrew in 2000, because the sound came from a common engine type and was not distinctive. Synthesizing a generic engine type's sound is unlikely to infringe a sound mark.

Under US law, facts such as published gear ratios, final drive and tyre sizes are not copyrightable (Feist, 1991); only creative selection or arrangement is. The EU/UK sui generis database right (15 years) blocks extracting or re-using a substantial part of a database that took substantial investment. Gear ratios should be compiled from primary sources rather than bulk-copied from one specs database.

Trademarkia shows 0 US and 0 EU results for TESBOX, TESBO and TESLABOX. Tesla, Inc. does not appear to own a BOOMBOX registration (82 BOOMBOX marks, all owned by others on the visible page). 'TES' word marks exist in class 9 (e.g., TES Global Ltd, education).

Third-party Tesla-oriented marks with a 'Tes-' prefix are registered in the US with no opposition shown: TESSIE (Tessie Technology LLC, EV-control software, classes 9/42, registered 7 May 2024), TESMANIAN (car accessories, classes 12/27) and TESERY (class 12).
Domains tesbox.com (live server, 404 at root), tesbox.app and tesbox.de (parked) and tesbox.io (parked, 'may be for sale') are already registered. tesbox.net did not resolve on 2026-10-05.

Hyundai Ioniq 5 N: N e-Shift simulates an 8-speed DCT with a hard rev limiter and a torque 'jolt' on shifts, using paddles, in manual or auto mode. N Active Sound+ plays 3 themes (Ignition = ICE N engine and exhaust; Evolution; Supersonic = fighter jet) through 8 interior Bose speakers and 2 exterior speakers, remixed by speed and throttle position. Exterior volume is capped 'within legal limits'.

Ioniq 5 N reception: reviewers say the fake gears are 'not just a gimmick', 'your brain is easily tricked', and the default sound (based on the i30 N 2.0 four-cylinder) convinces. The alternative sci-fi and jet sounds convince less, and it may make the car slightly slower. Hyundai is extending the feature to Ioniq 6 N and Ioniq 9 (Apr 2026); it is switchable and needs a minimum power level.

Dodge Charger Daytona Fratzonic Chambered Exhaust: exterior transducers plus passive radiators behind the bumper, up to 126 dB, driven by accelerator position, speed and torque. Owners complain it only has on/off tied to drive modes and that some sounds are poor; a Minnesota owner reportedly got a loud-muffler ticket.

BMW IconicSounds Electric (with Hans Zimmer) responds to pedal position and speed (in Expressive mode, chords arrive at 60 and 120 km/h). It deliberately does not imitate combustion engines, can be switched off, and its cabin sound in Personal/Comfort is the basis for the exterior pedestrian sound.
Mercedes sells 'Roaring Pulse' (an engine/turbine-like drive sound) for EQS/EQE as a paid OTA add-on, reportedly about $15/month or $150/year depending on region.

Competing Tesla-browser engine-sound web apps already exist. EV·ENGINE: free, GPS-only, 20 engines including brand-named recorded ones ('Ferrari 458', 'BMW M1 Procar'), offline after first load. Rombo: 7 generically named procedural engines, auto gearbox with blips, 'not affiliated with Tesla, Inc.'. EV Sound FX: $9.99/mo or $79.99/yr, 15+ generic sounds, manual/auto, and an optional external speaker sold separately.

Limitations stated by those apps: the Tesla browser reports position about once per second; GPS speed lags the speedometer; audio or sensors pause when the tab or page is hidden or backgrounded; setup should be done while parked.

Phone app 'Speedometers & Sounds of Cars' (iOS, 4.7 stars from 2.1K ratings) names sounds after real cars (Audi R8, BMW M5, Bugatti Veyron) with a disclaimer that they are 'only modeled on the original'. The main complaint is ads.

Tesla in-car browser: it is QtWebEngine (Chromium). In Drive, <video> is paused but audio continues, and WebAudio/WebGL/WebAssembly are available. A 2026 report says getUserMedia/mic is blocked. Since 2026.26, camera/mic work parked-only on AMD Ryzen cars and the engine moved to Chromium 148. Since 2026.20, parental controls can block the browser.
The Tesla browser needs Premium Connectivity over cellular (or Wi-Fi/hotspot), so offline-capable caching matters.

Steering wheel: rolling the left scroll wheel changes media volume and pressing it pauses/plays media. Browser audio can show in the media Miniplayer. A Tesbox 'upshift on scroll press' may therefore arrive as a media pause/play rather than a key event, or may pause the audio.
Tesla ended Model S and Model X production (announced 28 Jan 2026; last units 13 May 2026). The Cybertruck Long Range RWD was discontinued in Sep 2025.
Drag coefficients: Model 3 original 0.225, Highland 0.219; Model Y 0.23 (Juniper too), Model Y L 0.216. Model 3 uses a single-speed 9:1 reduction.

recommendations: Classify each car's audio by whether it has a subwoofer, not by model name: NO-SUB = Model 3 Highland base RWD 2023-25 (9 spk), Model Y RWD about Jan 2024-Jan 2025 (7 spk), Model 3/Y Standard Oct 2025+ (7 spk); SUB = all LR/Premium/Performance 3/Y, S, X, Cybertruck, Y L. Ask the user to confirm, because Tesla's own site once mislabelled the Model 3 RWD as having a subwoofer. Offer a parked 'bass check' test tone (e.g., 30/40/50/60 Hz) so the user can confirm.

NO-SUB bass chain: steep high-pass (about 4th order) around 45-55 Hz on the synth bus. Add harmonic-based virtual bass (regenerate harmonics 2-4 of the firing fundamental when it falls below about 60 Hz; the MaxxBass patent has expired). Follow with a soft-knee compressor and a brickwall limiter (about -1 dBFS ceiling). Cut the extra bass as volume rises, and add it back at low volume (equal-loudness compensation).

SUB bass chain: only a DC/infrasonic high-pass around 20-25 Hz plus the limiter. Let Tesla's own crossover send bass to the subwoofer. Cabin gain (+12 dB/oct below 70-90 Hz) means little bass boost is needed.

Default loudness: aim the engine sound at a few dB above about 67 dB highway cabin noise, not far above. Cap the default master so a typical drive stays well under 80 dBA on average (WHO 40 h/week). Show a hint never to mask sirens (StVO §23(1), Highway Code 148). Never route audio outside the car and never suggest external speakers (FMVSS 141, CA VC 27007).

Load estimation: per trim, store mass (US curb + about 75 kg occupant, or EU unladen), peak power and a_max derived from 0-100 time (a0 ≈ 27.78/t). Load ≈ clamp((m·a_measured + F_roadload(v)) / min(m·a0, P/v)). Cd values: 3 Highland 0.219, Y 0.23. Expose a Chill/Standard/Sport acceleration-mode setting, because the browser cannot detect it.

GPS arrives at about 1 Hz and lags the speedometer: interpolate or predict speed between fixes (e.g., a constant-acceleration Kalman filter) and smooth acceleration before using it as load. State the lag in the UI.

Touch UI while driving: large single-tap targets, no menus. Make Auto the default gearbox and the screen downshift optional with a clear warning (OLG Karlsruhe: touchscreen use while driving must be a brief glance only). Do all setup in Park.

Steering-wheel upshift: assume a scroll-wheel press may arrive as a media play/pause action rather than a key event. Test MediaSession handlers (play/pause/nexttrack/previoustrack) in the car, and guard against the press simply pausing the audio.

Engine naming: use generic archetype names (e.g., '2.5 L turbo inline-5', '5.0 L crossplane V8', '1.0 L triple'). Use no brand/model names as preset titles, no logos and no brand fonts. If referencing a real car in descriptive text, keep it minimal and factual ('inspired by the firing order of a 5-cylinder') and never claim the sound is the real car's.

Use 'Tesbox' only with a clear 'Not affiliated with or endorsed by Tesla, Inc.' disclaimer, no Tesla logo, T emblem, wordmark styling or 'Boombox' wording. Before launch, run a formal USPTO/EUIPO/WIPO clearance search: Trademarkia found nothing, but 'Tes-' plus 'box' may suggest a Tesla connection. tesbox.com/.app/.de/.io are taken, so choose another domain.

Gear ratio / final drive / tyre data: compile per car from primary manufacturer documents (brochures, press kits, homologation sheets). Do not bulk-extract from one specs database (EU/UK database right). Facts themselves are free to use in the US (Feist).

Offline PWA matters: browser data over cellular needs Premium Connectivity. Precache all code and assets on first load, and keep the page visible and in the foreground, since hidden or backgrounded tabs can suspend audio.

verdicts.claim: Model 3 Highland base RWD (2023-2025; UK/EU review) has 9 speakers and NO subwoofer. Layout: three 100 mm dash mids; in each front door a 25 mm tweeter and a 200 mm (8") woofer; 100 mm mids in the rear doors. Tesla's website once listed a subwoofer for this trim in error.
verdicts.evidence: TotallyEV (6 Mar 2024, UK) gives the 9-speaker layout as stated and adds: 'since our original review, Tesla has updated its website to state that there is no subwoofer in the new RWD Model 3.' Other sources agree that the RWD car has 9 speakers and no subwoofer: a Reddit thread ('No it doesn't'), an aftermarket kit sold as 'Model 3 Highland RWD 9 speakers', and a Brave index summary. The 9-speaker, no-subwoofer setup is not UK-only. US Model 3 RWD and Long Range RWD / 'Premium RWD' cars also have it (see 'missed'). The exact driver sizes come from a single reviewer who opened the car up. They are consistent with the PowerBass fitment guide (8-inch front-door woofer plus tweeter, 4-inch dash and rear-door speakers).

verdicts.claim: Model 3 Highland AWD/Long Range has 17 speakers, including two 200 mm upward-firing subwoofers in the boot and dual 200 mm woofers in each front door.
verdicts.evidence: The count of 17 with 2 subwoofers is confirmed independently. NotATeslaApp's comparison lists Model 3 Premium as '15 speakers' plus '2 subs', with Performance the same. EVSpecifications lists the 2026 Model 3 Performance as '15 x speakers, 2 x subwoofers'. Wikipedia says 'up to 17-speaker sound system (up from 14)'. The detailed layout (two 200 mm woofers per front door, two upward-firing 200 mm subwoofers in the boot, 60 mm door mids, parcel-shelf mids) comes from TotallyEV alone. Tesla does not publish it, and TotallyEV notes that Tesla 'hasn't confirmed all the details… total wattage also kept secret'. Treat the layout as medium confidence. Caveat: 'Long Range' does not mean subwoofer. The US Long Range RWD sold from mid-2024 (later 'Premium RWD') has the 9-speaker system with no subwoofer. The rule only holds for AWD and Performance.

verdicts.claim: 2026 Model 3 Performance (North America) is listed with 15 speakers plus 2 subwoofers.
verdicts.evidence: The EVSpecifications page cf4a406 is the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Performance AWD, North America, and lists '15 x speakers' and '2 x subwoofers'. NotATeslaApp's comparison, a separate source, gives Model 3 Performance the same audio as Premium AWD: 15 speakers and 2 subwoofers, so 17 drivers in total.

verdicts.claim: Model 3 Standard and Model Y Standard (launched 7 Oct 2025; US $36,990 / $39,990; also sold in Europe) have 7 speakers. The pricier versions have 15 speakers + 1 subwoofer. Standard trims also drop the rear screen, AM/FM radio and Autosteer (TACC only).

Three generalisations are wrong. (1) '15 speakers + 1 subwoofer' is the Model Y figure only. Model 3 Premium AWD and Performance have 15 speakers + 2 subwoofers. Model 3 Premium RWD has 9 speakers (Driving.ca: '2026 Tesla Model 3 Premium Rear-Wheel Drive … 9-speaker audio system'; Mashable: 'in the U.S. the Premium variant gets two speakers more'). (2) The European Standard trims launched on 5 Dec 2025 at €36,990 and €39,990, not 7 Oct. (3) The EU Model 3 Standard keeps FM/digital radio (Carscoops: 'spoils Europe with an FM radio') and keeps Basic Autopilot with Autosteer (Mashable). Losing radio and Autosteer is US-only.

The 15-speaker Premium system (Premium and Performance trims) is 3 tweeters, 9 mids, 2 woofers and 1 subwoofer (8", 160 W), with 2 amps (~560 W). Immersive Sound and a separate subwoofer level are Premium-only.
verdicts.evidence: The breakdown comes only from a BimmerTech blog post (29 Apr 2026). BimmerTech sells aftermarket upgrades, and the post cites no sources. No Tesla source publishes driver types or wattage. Two points conflict with other evidence. (a) Tesla's own spec text for the 2024 7-speaker Model Y RWD, quoted by Electrek, read 'Custom audio – 7 speakers, 1 amp, and immersive sound'. So Immersive Sound was offered on at least one 7-speaker system, which contradicts 'Premium-only'. (b) BimmerTech counts the subwoofer inside the 15. TechCrunch and NotATeslaApp say '15 speakers and one subwoofer', which reads as 16 drivers. The likely 7-speaker layout is consistent with TotallyEV's pre-Highland Model 3 standard layout (two 8-inch door woofers, three 4-inch dash units, two 4-inch rear-door units) and with the 'center tweeter' PowerBass mentions in the dash. That support is circumstantial.

verdicts.evidence: Electrek (8 Jan 2024): before, 13 speakers, 1 subwoofer, 2 amps; after, 'Custom audio – 7 speakers, 1 amp, and immersive sound'; RWD only, with Dual Motor and Performance unchanged. Carscoops (10 Jan 2024) independently reports 13 to 7 speakers, the subwoofer removed and 2 amps cut to 1, on the US Model Y RWD only. Neither report clearly says whether the '13' included the subwoofer. The 'immersive sound' part of Tesla's wording contradicts the Premium-only claim in the claim above.

verdicts.evidence: Car and Driver's Model X spec sheet reads 'premium 22-speaker (960-watt) audio system w/active road noise reduction'. Tesla's January 2021 refresh text, quoted on Reddit, reads 'A 22-speaker, 960-watt audio system … new microphones enable active noise canceling'. CarBuzz says the same for the Model S Plaid. The noise reduction feature arrived by over-the-air update in December 2021 (InsideEVs, TorqueNews). It uses microphones in the front headrests and plays 'anti-noise' through the speakers. Tesla does not say how many of the 22 are subwoofers. Caveat: production of Model S and Model X ended on 13 May 2026, so these are installed-base cars only.

verdicts.claim: Cybertruck has 15 speakers, including 2 dedicated subwoofers (reported as 8" units under the rear bench), with distributed amplifiers.
verdicts.evidence: TorqueNews (10 Feb 2024), citing Tesla's spec page: '15 speakers, 2 dedicated subwoofers' with distributed amplifiers. Separate sources: Autoevolution (Jun 2023 and Sep 2024) describes 'two 8" subwoofers with small enclosures under the rear seat', ported and aimed forward, and Cybertruck Owners Club says '2x 8 inch subwoofers below rear seat'. PowerBass lists its 8-inch OE8C-T3Y as a fit for the Cybertruck front doors. The subwoofer size comes from press and forum reports, not from Tesla.

verdicts.claim: Model 3 (2018-2024 and Highland), Model Y (2020-2025 and Juniper) and Cybertruck all use 8" (4 ohm) front-door woofers. A drop-in replacement (PowerBass OE8C-T3Y) is rated 50 Hz-21 kHz. The 4" dash/rear-door replacements are rated 95 Hz-21 kHz. Practical door-woofer bass floor is therefore about 50 Hz, and the rear 4" speakers should get no deep bass.
verdicts.evidence: The datasheet facts are confirmed from the PowerBass PDF itself. OE8C-T3Y: 8-inch, 4 Ω, 50 Hz–21 kHz, 87 dB, 90/180 W, fits Model 3 2018-24, Model Y 2020-25, Cybertruck, Model Y Juniper and Model 3 Highland. OE42-T3Y and OE40CN-T3Y: 4-inch, 4 Ω, 95 Hz–21 kHz. OE40CW-T3Y is rated 95 Hz–10 kHz, not 21 kHz. The PDF also says 'Cybertruck, Highland, and Juniper Models have additional fitments or locations that we do not support'. The conclusion does not follow from these figures. An aftermarket driver's marketing frequency range, with no tolerance stated and no enclosure or cabin given, tells us nothing about Tesla's own driver or Tesla's DSP high-pass. Cabin gain (about 12 dB/octave below roughly 70-90 Hz, see the cabin-gain claim) would push the in-cabin floor below a free-air 50 Hz figure. An indexed TotallyEV summary says the no-subwoofer Model 3 'lacks the deep sub-bass extension (below 45Hz)'. That summary is low confidence. No measured in-cabin response for a Tesla without a subwoofer was found. Treat ~50 Hz as a guess, not a hard floor.

verdicts.claim: Car cabin gain adds roughly 12 dB/octave of bass reinforcement below a 'transfer frequency' of about 70-90 Hz. Smaller cabins get it at higher frequencies.
verdicts.evidence: The claim is widely repeated in car-audio sources: CarAudioHelp, Audio Intensity's acoustics and DSP guides ('rises at approximately 12 dB per octave below 80 Hz'), and a Trinituner forum post copying CarAudioHelp. All are trade blogs with no measurement data, and they repeat one another. No primary acoustics paper, OEM measurement or Tesla-specific measurement was found. The physics agrees on direction, since cabin dimensions are small next to bass wavelengths (CarAudioHelp: 40 Hz is about 28 ft against a cabin about 12 ft long). 12 dB/octave is the ideal sealed-cabin figure, and real cabins leak, so it should be treated as an upper bound. The point that smaller cabins have a higher transfer frequency and more gain is stated consistently.

verdicts.claim: Car-audio practice for systems without a subwoofer is to high-pass door speakers around 60-80 Hz: about 80 Hz for 6.5" door mid-bass and about 60 Hz for 8" door woofers.
verdicts.evidence: Audio Intensity's crossover guide does give 80 Hz LR4 for 6.5-inch mid-bass and 60 Hz LR4 for an 8-inch door woofer. It describes the 8-inch as working 'as a bandpass component between the subwoofer and midrange layers', which is a setup with a subwoofer, not without one. The second source cited (Crutchfield) could not be fetched (403). No source was found showing that systems without a subwoofer high-pass door woofers at 60-80 Hz. Doing so would remove nearly all bass, so the usual practice there is to run the doors full-range with only a protective subsonic filter. Tesbox also cannot reach Tesla's crossovers or DSP. It can only filter its own output.

verdicts.claim: Four-stroke engine firing frequency is f = rpm x cylinders / 120 Hz, with harmonics at integer multiples. Examples: 4-cyl at 800 rpm = 26.7 Hz; 5-cyl at 850 rpm = 35 Hz; V8 at 700 rpm = 46.7 Hz. Idle fundamentals fall below the about 50 Hz door-woofer limit.
verdicts.evidence: The formula is confirmed (MufflerDesigner: Freq = (RPM/120)·Cn·n; one combustion per cylinder every 2 crank revolutions). The arithmetic is correct: 800·4/120 = 26.67, 850·5/120 = 35.4, 700·8/120 = 46.67. The firing order (cylinders/2) is the dominant component. The 'about 50 Hz limit' rests on the unverified claim above. The 'integer multiples of the firing frequency' model is also incomplete. Uneven-firing engines repeat only every 720°, so they produce half-order components at multiples of rpm/120, below the firing frequency. Example: crossplane V8 banks fire at intervals of '180-90-180-270 crankshaft degrees', which produces the 'burble' (Wikipedia, Crossplane).

verdicts.claim: Virtual bass (the 'missing fundamental' effect): adding harmonics of frequencies below the speaker's cutoff makes listeners hear the low pitch through small speakers (Larsen & Aarts, JAES 50(3):147-164, 2002). Waves' MaxxBass patent US5930373 (priority 4 Apr 1997) expired 4 Apr 2017, so the technique is free to use.
verdicts.evidence: TU/e research portal: Erik Larsen & Ronald M. Aarts, 'Reproducing low-pitched signals through small loudspeakers', J. Audio Eng. Soc. 50(3):147-164, 2002, about psychoacoustic methods using non-linear processing. Google Patents for US5930373A (K S Waves Ltd; Shashoua, Glotter): filed and prioritised 4 Apr 1997, granted 27 Jul 1999, status 'Expired - Lifetime', adjusted expiry 4 Apr 2017. It covers making the brain hear bass from generated harmonics. Caveat: only this patent has expired. Later virtual-bass patents (from Waves and others) may cover specific refinements, so 'free to use' should read 'the basic technique is free to use'. A freedom-to-operate check would be needed for any copied refinement.

verdicts.claim: Car and Driver measured a Model 3 Highland Long Range RWD at 67 dB average at a 70 mph cruise, about 3 dB quieter than the pre-facelift car, thanks to acoustic-laminated glass all round.
verdicts.evidence: Car and Driver (14 Oct 2024), fetched through a reader proxy: the 2024 Model 3 Long Range RWD averaged 67 dB at a 70-mph cruise, against 70 dB for the 2019 Dual Motor Long Range they tested before. The glass is 'acoustic-laminated (double-pane) glass all around; previously, only the windshield and front side glass were laminated.' Car and Driver also credits a reshaped hood and new Michelin Primacy All Season tyres, so the glass is not the only reason. The car tested was the US Long Range RWD, which has the 9-speaker system without a subwoofer. A 2026 Model Y Standard (RWD) review measured 66 dB.

corrections: Model 3 'Premium' or 'Long Range' does not mean a subwoofer. The US Model 3 Long Range RWD (mid-2024 on, later sold as 'Premium RWD') has the 9-speaker system with no subwoofer. Tesla changed its documentation from 'Long Range and Performance' to AWD-only for premium audio (Reddit, 1 Aug 2024), and Driving.ca lists the 2026 Model 3 Premium RWD as 9-speaker. Only Model 3 AWD and Performance have 15 speakers + 2 subwoofers. The summary line 'Model 3 LR/Premium/Performance (17 speakers, 2x8-inch subwoofers)' is wrong for LR/Premium RWD.

On the more expensive trims, Model 3 AWD and Performance have 15 speakers + 2 subwoofers, while Model Y Premium and Performance have 15 speakers + 1 subwoofer. TechCrunch's '15 speakers and one subwoofer' is the Model Y figure.

The European Standard trims launched on 5 Dec 2025 (€36,990 for Model 3, €39,990 for Model Y), not 7 Oct 2025. The EU Model 3 Standard keeps FM/digital radio and Basic Autopilot with Autosteer. Losing radio and Autosteer is a US-only change. Sources conflict on the cheapest EU Model 3 Premium: Mashable says 7 speakers, Carscoops says 9.

Tesla's own 2024 spec for the 7-speaker Model Y RWD read 'Custom audio – 7 speakers, 1 amp, and immersive sound'. Immersive Sound is therefore not proven Premium-only. Detect a subwoofer through a user setting or a listening test rather than relying on that UI option.

The PowerBass OE40CW-T3Y is rated 95 Hz–10 kHz, not 21 kHz. A 50 Hz rating for an aftermarket driver says nothing about the stock driver or Tesla's DSP high-pass, so treat ~50 Hz as a guess, not a measured floor.

Car-audio advice to high-pass door speakers at 60-80 Hz assumes a subwoofer is present. Without one, doors normally run full-range with only a subsonic filter. Tesbox cannot change Tesla's crossovers or DSP. It can only filter and shape its own output.
Car and Driver's 3 dB comparison is against a 2019 Dual Motor Long Range (70 dB). The reduction also comes from the reshaped hood and new tyres, not only the glass.

The firing-frequency model needs half-order components (multiples of rpm/120) for uneven-firing engines and for exhaust pulses per bank (crossplane V8, odd-fire), not only integer multiples of rpm·cyl/120.
missed: Tesla Model S and Model X are discontinued. Musk said 2026 would be the final model year, the last units left Fremont on 13 May 2026, and the line was repurposed for Optimus. They remain installed-base cars, so keep them in the model picker (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Model_S, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Model_X).

Pre-Highland Model 3 (2017-2023): the Standard Range / SR+ had 8 speakers, later 7, with no subwoofer: two 8-inch 80 W front-door woofers, three 4-inch 33 W dash mids and 4-inch rear-door mids. The LR/Performance had 15, later 14, with a trunk subwoofer, two amps and about 605 W (TotallyEV, https://totallyev.net/tesla-model-3-audio-review-standard-vs-premium-audio-comparison/). The car picker needs these older trims too.

Speaker setup varies within the same model, year and trim name, by market (US vs EU) and by build date (the Model Y RWD cut in Jan 2024, the Model 3 LR RWD in 2024). A model/year picker cannot reliably say whether a subwoofer is fitted. Tesbox should ask 'subwoofer: yes/no/unsure' and could add a low-frequency test sweep.

Electrek's 2026 Model Y Standard (RWD) review describes the 7-speaker system as 'muffled, heavy on bass, and light on mids'. Cabin noise was 66 dB, against 67 dB in Car and Driver's Model 3 Highland LR RWD test. Without a subwoofer the door woofers still produce noticeable bass, so the app may need to boost mids more than bass in these cars (https://electrek.co/2026/08/03/2026-tesla-model-y-rwd-review/).

Model S/X have Active Road Noise Reduction: front-headrest microphones measure cabin noise and the system plays anti-noise through the speakers (owner's manual via TeslaOracle; InsideEVs Dec 2021). How it interacts with synthetic low-frequency engine audio is undocumented. Test with ARNR on and off (https://www.teslaoracle.com/2021/06/15/a-deep-dive-inside-the-tesla-model-s-plaid-ui-yoke-interior-anc-more/, https://insideevs.com/news/555369/tesla-active-road-noise-reduction/).

The PowerBass guide says Cybertruck, Highland and Juniper have 'additional fitments or locations' it does not support. These newer cars have more drivers than the older Model 3/Y layout (https://powerbassusa.com/media/uploads_file/2025/08/13/a689d30a14704e8.91360818.pdf).
Model Y L: 19 speakers, a subwoofer and 2 extra overhead speakers (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Model_Y). The researcher's summary mentions it, but no claim was submitted for it.
